articles.title: Logtide: 1 Year After the First Commit (The Real Numbers)
articles.description: On November 26, 2025 I pushed a commit called "Initial Commit - LogWard v0.1.0 alpha". Four days...
articles.body_html:
On November 26, 2025 I pushed a commit called "Initial Commit - LogWard v0.1.0 alpha". Four days later I published a post on dev.to titled I built an Open Source Datadog alternative because ELK was eating my RAM. It had a Docker Compose file, a SvelteKit 5 frontend, TimescaleDB instead of Elasticsearch, and Redis with BullMQ for the job queue.

That was a year ago. In January I wrote a 2-months post with every number I had, good and bad. This is the same exercise at twelve months. Same rule as last time: no bullshit, just numbers.

The numbers

Launch (Nov 2025) 2 months (Jan 2026) 1 year (Nov 2026)
GitHub stars 0 223 457
Docker pulls (backend image) 0 3,000+ 47,000+
Commits 1 n/a 2,020
Releases 0.1.0 0.4.x 50+, latest 1.6.0
Issues opened 0 27 103
Merged PRs from other people 0 1 17
Storage engines 1 1 3
Official SDKs 3 5 7

The stars curve flattened after the virtualizationhowto.com spike. The Docker pulls curve did not. Fifteen times more pulls with only twice the stars tells me what I suspected at two months: the people running Logtide are mostly not the people starring repos. They are self-hosters who pull an image, put it behind a reverse proxy, and never open an issue unless something breaks.

The commit count is mostly me. 1,982 of the 2,020 commits have my name on them. The remaining ones are small, but they are the ones I remember.

The year in releases

A quick timeline, because a year of changelogs is long and nobody should read it.

  • January: forced rebrand from LogWard to Logtide after a trademark conflict. 0.4.0 shipped the same week.
  • January / February: 0.5.0 made Redis optional. 0.6.0 added PII masking at ingestion, and ClickHouse as a second storage engine.
  • February: 0.7.0 added OTLP metrics, service maps and audit logs. Logs, traces and metrics in one place.
  • March: 0.8.0 added MongoDB as a third storage engine, plus browser observability.
  • April: 0.9.0 replaced the fixed dashboard with custom dashboards, added uptime monitoring with public status pages, and log parsing pipelines.
  • June: 1.0.0. More on what that release actually was below.
  • July / August: inbound webhook receivers, digest emails, error regression detection, geo map panels.
  • October: 1.6.0, the biggest release of the year. A rebuilt UI, one query language that works on every storage engine, an incidents inbox, Slack, Teams and PagerDuty destinations, and an extension system.

What I got wrong in the 2-months post

Re-reading the January post is a bit uncomfortable. A few things I wrote with confidence turned out to be wrong.

"OpenTelemetry metrics: postponed indefinitely." Only two users had asked for it, and I wrote that most people use Prometheus anyway. Six weeks later 0.7.0 shipped OTLP metrics. Logs, traces and metrics in one place turned out to matter more than a vote count in an issue tracker. The lesson I wrote at the time was "build what users request". It still holds, but it is not the whole picture.

"TimescaleDB was the right choice." It still is, as the default. But by March Logtide also ran on ClickHouse (0.6) and MongoDB (0.8), through a storage layer called reservoir. The cost was real: every query, every filter and every panel now has to behave identically on three engines. Getting that right took until 1.6.0, where the same search syntax finally parses to the same results everywhere.

"Redis might be unnecessary. Next version might remove it." This one I got right, mostly. Since 0.5.0 Redis is optional: without it, the job queue runs on PostgreSQL through graphile-worker. It is not removed: if you already run Redis, BullMQ is still there. Making a dependency optional turned out to be more useful than deleting it.

What 1.0 actually was

At 0.9.0 I wrote that we were not jumping straight to a 1.0 declaration, because we wanted the announcement to mean something.

What it ended up meaning was a security audit. Before cutting 1.0, I went through every data access path in the backend looking for one specific thing: a query that could read another organization's data. I found some. The logs and traces query APIs accepted a projectId parameter and trusted it without checking that it belonged to the API key making the request. There were also tenant-table queries missing an organization filter, protected only by the route above them.

All of it was fixed in 1.0, along with a dedicated isolation test suite and CI checks so the same pattern fails the build if it comes back. PII masking also became fail-closed: before 1.0, if a masking rule threw, the batch was stored unmasked with a warning in the console. For a product whose whole pitch is GDPR, that was the worst possible failure mode.

Then, right after 1.0, a batch of issues was reported privately through coordinated disclosure by KIberblick.de, including a cross-tenant read on the dashboard endpoints and a stored XSS. Fixed in 1.0.3. I am genuinely grateful for that report. It is humbling to run an audit and then have someone else find what you missed a week later, but that is the system working.

The lesson I'd give anyone building a multi-tenant product solo: the hard part is not the features. It is making sure every single query is scoped, and keeping it that way while you ship features fast.

What worked

Shipping small and often. 53 tags in a year is roughly one a week. Most were boring patch releases. Boring patch releases are what make people trust a project enough to upgrade it.

Docker Compose as the main install path. I said at two months that Docker Compose working in five minutes got more stars than any feature. That is still true. There is a Helm chart now, but the Compose file is what most people use.

Writing about the technical decisions, not the product. The most read posts I wrote this year were not the release announcements. I Replaced Redis with PostgreSQL got 340 reactions, the microservices math got 154. The average release post got around 15. People came for the Postgres opinions, and some of them found the log management along the way.

SDKs in the languages people actually use. Node.js, Python, PHP, Kotlin/Java, C#, Go and Ruby, plus Laravel, Symfony, Slim and WordPress integrations. The Kotlin SDK was a community contribution in the first two months, and I still think about that every time someone asks for a new language.

What didn't

The rebrand. I covered it in January, but it is worth repeating because it is the cheapest lesson on this page: check the trademark before you name anything.

Doing everything alone. 98% of the commits are mine. That is fast, but it means every architectural mistake is mine too, and there is nobody to say "this is a bad idea" before it ships. The extension system in 1.6.0 is partly an answer to that: a way for people to build on Logtide without having to get a PR through me.

Thank you

To everyone who opened an issue, especially the ones that started with "this is probably a dumb question" and were not. To the 17 merged pull requests that did not come from me. To the people who reported security issues privately instead of on Twitter. And to the self-hosters running Logtide somewhere I will never see, who never open an issue because nothing is broken. You are the reason the Docker pull counter keeps moving.

If you're using Logtide, I'd love to hear how. Open a discussion, open an issue, or drop a ⭐ if it has been useful.

  • 🌐 Cloud: logtide.dev
  • 💻 GitHub: logtide-dev/logtide
  • 📖 Docs: logtide.dev/docs

Here's to year two. 🌊

articles.title: My Harness Reported 0 Findings on 100 Files. All 100 Were Ignored.
articles.description: Three separate mechanisms make an ESLint run report zero while reading nothing — and every one of them exits 0 with an empty stderr. A clean bill of health and a file nobody opened are the same output.
articles.body_html:
I ran fourteen lint rules over 100 files and got back zero findings. Every
rule silent, clean sweep, nothing to fix.

The correct answer was 308 findings in 54 of those files. The harness had read
none of them, exited 0, and printed nothing to stderr.

Here are the three ways that happens, all of them measured this week, all of
them silent.

1. The files were outside the base path

ESLint resolves what it is allowed to lint relative to cwd. Point it at a
directory that is not under the cwd of the process, and every file comes back
ignored:

File ignored because outside of base path.

That string arrives as a message with a null ruleId — the same shape as a
parse error. If your loop counts messages.filter(m => m.ruleId), or skips
files whose messages look unfamiliar, you have just discarded the only
explanation you were given.

On the CLI it is quieter still. Exit code 0. Empty stderr.

Fix: set cwd to the tree you are measuring.

2. The .ts files were never eligible

Flat config (ESLint 9.39.2 here) matches files by pattern. Omit files, and
the default covers .js and friends — not .ts, in an ecosystem that is
mostly TypeScript.

// eslint.config.mjs
export default [{ rules: { "no-eval": "error" } }];

src/a.ts   ← contains eval()
src/b.js   ← clean

$ eslint .
$ echo $?
0

No output. Exit 0. The .ts file contains eval() and was never opened.

This one is worse than the first, because a partial corpus still produces
plausible numbers. A repository that is 80% TypeScript reports on the other
20% and calls it a result.

Fix: files: ['**/*.ts', '**/*.tsx'], explicitly, and check the count of files
actually linted against a count you obtained some other way.

3. The build under test was not the build you ship

In a monorepo, node_modules/<your-package> is usually a symlink into the
workspace. Anything you measure through it is unreleased source.

I asked a plugin which of its rules carry a fixer. From the workspace:

prefer-event-target: code

From the published package, same command, clean directory:

prefer-event-target: no fixer

Both true. Different questions. I nearly published a correction to a correct
article on the strength of the first one.

Fix: measure in a scratch directory with an npm i <pkg>@<exact-version>, and
say which tree the number came from.

Why all three survive review

Nothing throws. Nothing warns. The exit code is 0 in every case — and the one
time I saw a 1, it came from a real finding in a file that was linted, not
from the file that was skipped. "It exited non-zero, so it noticed" is the
wrong conclusion and I drew it once.

They also fail at three different layers — which files are eligible, which
eligible files are covered, and which build is under test — so fixing one
leaves the others exactly as they were.

And they all fail toward good news. There is no version of these bugs that
invents findings. That asymmetry is what makes them survive: a number that is
too high gets investigated, and a number that is too low gets celebrated.

The check

One rule, before you believe any of it: write the code the tool must flag,
and make sure it flags it.

export function C({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  return <ul style={{ color: "red" }}>
    {items.map((i) => <li key={i} onClick={() => log(i)}>{i}</li>)}
  </ul>;
}

Four lines, tripping at least two of the rules under test. If the canary is
silent, the corpus number is not a number.

That is what caught mine. The hundred-file zero was completely believable —
it was the four-line file reporting zero that was not.

A count from an instrument you have never seen fail is not a measurement, it is
a hope.

This is the cheap half of what ground truth catches that unit tests miss:
the tests all passed, because the harness they exercised was working — it was
the corpus it pointed at that was empty. It is also why a result you cannot
re-run is not yet a result, which is the whole distinction between
reproducibility and replicability.
And a zero that means "read nothing" corrupts the one cell every other metric
is derived from — the true-negative box of the confusion matrix.

Part of the Interlace ESLint ecosystem. Source on GitHub · Follow: Dev.to/ofri-peretz

What's the last clean report you got — and would you know if the tool had read nothing?

articles.title: You're Still Writing CSS Like It's 2015: The Modern Architecture Guide That Fixes Specificity Forever
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into modern CSS architecture. Learn how browsers execute the layout and composite pipeline, how Cascade Layers eliminate specificity wars forever, how container queries replace media queries, and how content-visibility yields instant 10x DOM performance.
articles.body_html:
For nearly two decades, one running joke has united frontend developers more than any other:

The Peter Griffin Venetian blinds GIF, where one adjustment causes the entire structure to collapse into chaotic ruin, captioned: "CSS in a nutshell."

Almost every developer has fought that exact battle. You write a clean class rule to style a button. Nothing happens. You check the browser developer tools and find that a deeply nested rule written three years ago (#app .sidebar .widget .button) is silently overriding your declaration. In frustration, you add another class. It still fails. Finally, you surrender to the universal escape hatch:

background-color: #3b82f6 !important;

It is this endless struggle with selector specificity, global scope leakage, and unpredictable side effects that drove the industry toward BEM conventions, CSS Modules, CSS-in-JS runtimes, and utility frameworks.

Developers convinced themselves that CSS itself was fundamentally flawed.

Yet CSS was never broken. The reality is simpler: most developers were taught CSS as a collection of cosmetic styling rules rather than a layout calculation engine executed by a browser rendering pipeline.

Over the past three years, CSS has undergone its most dramatic architectural evolution since the introduction of Flexbox and Grid. With native Cascade Layers (@layer), Container Queries (@container), Relational Selectors (:has()), and Render Containment (content-visibility), modern CSS has solved the exact architectural problems that once required megabytes of JavaScript tooling.

Here is what actually happens across the browser rendering engine when it parses and renders your CSS.

1. The Browser Rendering Pipeline: Style, Layout, Paint, and Composite

To write high-performance CSS and debug unexpected visual bugs, you must understand how a browser engine (such as Blink in Chrome, Gecko in Firefox, or WebKit in Safari) converts raw text into pixels on a screen.

The rendering process is not a single instantaneous step. It is a strict multi-stage pipeline.

Stage 1: Recalculate Style (DOM + CSSOM = Render Tree)

First, the browser parses the HTML into the Document Object Model (DOM) and the stylesheet text into the CSS Object Model (CSSOM).

The engine traverses the DOM tree and matches CSS selectors against every node. It resolves specificity, inheritance, and cascade rules to calculate the computed style for every element.

Nodes that have display: none or represent metadata (<head>, <script>) are omitted entirely. The resulting output is the Render Tree, a tree of visible render objects.

Stage 2: Layout (Reflow)

Once the engine knows which styles apply to which elements, it must determine their geometry: exact pixel widths, heights, margins, paddings, and screen coordinates.

Starting at the root of the Render Tree, the browser evaluates box sizing, flex distributions, grid tracks, and font metrics.

Layout is mathematically expensive. Because child elements depend on parent dimensions and parent dimensions often depend on child contents, a layout calculation on one element can trigger a cascading recalculation across the entire document tree. This recalculation is known as a Reflow.

Stage 3: Paint (Rasterization)

With exact coordinates calculated, the browser converts vector boxes into actual colored pixels.

During the Paint phase, the engine records drawing commands for backgrounds, borders, text, shadows, and colors into memory buffers. It does not draw everything onto a single canvas; it divides the page into multiple independent graphics layers (such as fixed headers, scrolling containers, and canvas elements).

Stage 4: Composite (GPU Execution)

Finally, the browser uploads these rasterized layers as textures to the Graphical Processing Unit (GPU).

The GPU Compositor calculates layer transformations, opacity blending, and clipping, outputting the final 60fps or 120fps image directly to your display screen.

The 60fps Golden Rule

Understanding this pipeline explains why animating certain CSS properties feels silky smooth, while animating others stutters:

  • Animating left, top, width, or margin: Triggers Layout ➔ Paint ➔ Composite. Every frame forces the CPU to recalculate document geometry and repaint pixels across the main thread.
  • Animating transform or opacity: Completely bypasses Layout and Paint! The browser simply hands matrix math and alpha values directly to the GPU Compositor.

If an animation does not alter geometry, never animate properties that trigger Reflow.

2. Cascade Layers (@layer): The End of Specificity Wars

For twenty years, CSS specificity was a zero-sum arms race.

Selectors were scored using an immutable tuple formula: (Inline, IDs, Classes, Elements). If a third-party UI library declared .card .header button, your custom .primary-btn class could never override it without artificially chaining classes or resorting to !important.

CSS Cascade Layers (@layer) completely rewrite how the cascade operates.

The Paradigm Shift: Layer Precedence Over Selector Weight

Before Cascade Layers, selector specificity reigned supreme. With @layer, layer order overrides selector specificity entirely.

A low-specificity selector in a higher layer will unconditionally defeat a high-specificity selector in a lower layer:

/* Explicit layer order definition */
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer components {
  /* High specificity: 1 ID, 2 Classes (1-2-0) */
  #main-nav .menu-list .nav-link {
    color: #475569;
    font-weight: 500;
  }
}

@layer utilities {
  /* Low specificity: 1 Class (0-1-0) */
  .text-danger {
    color: #ef4444;
  }
}

In the example above, an element with both classes will be colored #ef4444 (red).

Why? Because the utilities layer was defined after the components layer. The browser does not even evaluate selector specificity between the two rules; it resolves layer precedence first. Specificity only matters as a tiebreaker within the same layer.

The Cascade Hierarchy and Resolution Mechanics

The browser evaluates styling rules according to this strict priority chain:

  1. !important User Agent styles
  2. !important User styles
  3. !important Layered Author styles (Inverted order: earlier layers win when marked important!)
  4. !important Unlayered Author styles
  5. Normal Unlayered Author styles (Styles outside any @layer block always win against layered styles)
  6. Normal Layered Author styles (Evaluated by layer declaration order)
  7. Normal User styles
  8. Normal User Agent styles (Browser defaults)

Notice rule 5: unlayered styles always override layered styles. This makes adopting Cascade Layers zero-risk for legacy applications: you can wrap third-party design systems or reset sheets in @layer vendor, reset;, and all of your existing application CSS will effortlessly take precedence.

3. Container Queries: Escaping the Viewport Trap

When Ethan Marcotte coined Responsive Web Design in 2010, the viewport was the only container that mattered. We wrote @media (min-width: 768px) because tablets had wider screens than phones.

Modern web architecture is not built around whole pages; it is built around modular component systems.

Consider a ProductCard component. In your application, that card might appear:

  • As a full-width hero card in the main feed (800px wide).
  • Inside a narrow sidebar column on the desktop dashboard (280px wide).
  • Inside a medium drawer modal (450px wide).

If you style that card using @media (min-width: 1024px), the card will assume it has 1024px of screen space, even when squished inside a 280px sidebar. It will render its desktop horizontal layout, breaking your sidebar layout completely.

Container Queries (@container) solve this by measuring the component's immediate parent container rather than the browser window.

Registering a Containment Context

To enable container queries on an element, you declare its containment type using container-type:

.card-wrapper {
  /* Informs the layout engine to track this element's width */
  container-type: inline-size;
  container-name: card-container;
}

Setting container-type: inline-size informs the browser's layout engine to track the horizontal width of .card-wrapper as a containment boundary.

Now, child elements query .card-wrapper directly:

.product-card {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 12px;
}

/* When the parent container is at least 500px wide */
@container card-container (min-width: 500px) {
  .product-card {
    flex-direction: row;
    align-items: center;
  }

  .product-image {
    width: 200px;
    height: 100%;
  }
}

The Architectural Benefit: True Component Autonomy

With container queries, components become truly portable. You can drop the same ProductCard into a mobile viewport, a desktop three-column grid, a sidebar, or an off-canvas drawer. The card self-adapts to the space allocated to it by its layout parent, with zero JavaScript resize observers.

4. Modern Selectors: The Power of :has(), :is(), and :where()

For decades, CSS selectors could only travel down the DOM tree. You could style a child based on its parent (.parent .child), but you could never style a parent based on its children.

Developers wrote extensive JavaScript event handlers just to toggle a .has-error class on a parent form whenever an input became invalid.

CSS relational selectors have completely removed this limitation.

The :has() Parent Selector Engine

The :has() pseudo-class allows an element to inspect its descendants or adjacent siblings:

/* Style an entire card container if it contains an image */
.card:has(img) {
  grid-template-rows: 240px auto;
}

/* Highlight a form fieldset when any radio button inside is checked */
fieldset:has(input[type="radio"]:checked) {
  border-color: #3b82f6;
  background-color: #eff6ff;
}

/* Style previous navigation items when a sibling is hovered */
nav li:hover + li {
  opacity: 0.8;
}

Internally, browser engines optimize :has() using bloom filter caches and invalidation sets. Rather than re-evaluating the entire DOM tree on every click, the engine tracks which elements observe descendant mutations, restricting style recalculations to localized subtrees.

:is() vs :where(): The Specificity Split

When grouping complex selector lists, modern CSS provides two pseudo-classes: :is() and :where().

They accept identical syntax, but handle specificity in opposite ways:

/* :is() adopts the specificity of its most specific argument */
:is(header, main, #special-footer) h1 {
  /* Specificity includes the ID selector (#special-footer): 1-0-1 */
  font-size: 2rem;
}

/* :where() ALWAYS has exactly ZERO specificity (0-0-0) */
:where(header, main, #special-footer) h1 {
  /* Specificity is purely from 'h1': 0-0-1 (the contents of :where() count as 0!) */
  font-size: 2rem;
}

:where() is the ultimate tool for design system authors. By wrapping default reset styles and base components inside :where(), you guarantee that any developer consuming your library can override your styles with a single plain class name, without specificity battles.

5. Rendering Performance: content-visibility and Containment

Modern web applications often render massive documents: social feeds with hundreds of posts, e-commerce catalog grids with thousands of products, or long technical documentation pages.

When a browser loads a page with 3,000 DOM elements, it parses, calculates layout, and rasters painting commands for every single element, even though the user can only see the first five on their screen.

This creates significant Total Blocking Time (TBT) and delays First Contentful Paint.

content-visibility provides an instant, native fix.

How content-visibility: auto Works

Adding a single CSS rule instructs the browser engine to skip layout and painting for elements currently outside the viewport:

.feed-post {
  /* Skip rendering work when offscreen */
  content-visibility: auto;

  /* Provide an estimated height to prevent scrollbar jumping */
  contain-intrinsic-size: 0 450px;
}

When an element with content-visibility: auto is offscreen:

  1. Rendering Bypass: The browser treats its contents as if they have display: none for rendering purposes. It skips layout calculations, font rasterization, and painting work.
  2. Accessible DOM: Unlike display: none, the element remains in the DOM tree! Screen readers, in-page search (Ctrl+F), and DOM querying APIs can still access it.
  3. Just-In-Time Rendering: As the user scrolls toward the element, the browser seamlessly executes layout and paint right before it enters the viewport.

The companion property, contain-intrinsic-size: 0 450px, tells the layout engine to reserve 450px of vertical space while the real content is unrendered. This prevents the browser scrollbar from jumping erratically as offscreen elements load.

In real-world production benchmarks, applying content-visibility: auto to large lists frequently reduces initial rendering and layout time by over 70 percent.

6. Three Common Modern CSS Traps (And the Internal Fixes)

As frontend developers adopt modern CSS features, three subtle architectural pitfalls frequently cause production bugs:

Trap 1: The Circular Container Query Reflow Loop

If a container's size depends on its children, and its children change size based on container queries, an infinite layout loop can occur:

/* CAUSES LAYOUT THRASHING OR BLANK DISPLAY */
.container {
  /* Tracking both width AND height */
  container-type: size;
  height: auto; /* Child content determines height! */
}

The browser cannot compute the container's height because it needs child dimensions, but child dimensions depend on container queries against that height. The engine detects the circular dependency and forces the dimension to 0px.

The Fix: Always use container-type: inline-size unless the container has an explicit, fixed block height set in pixels or viewport units.

Trap 2: The :has() Performance Degradation in Deep DOMs

While :has() is highly optimized, using broad, unbounded descendant queries inside frequently mutated animations will cause main thread frame drops:

/* SLOW: Checks every single descendant in the entire DOM tree */
body:has(*) { ... }

/* FAST: Scoped to immediate children or localized subtrees */
.form-group:has(> input:focus) { ... }

The Fix: Always scope :has() to a specific component container, and prefer child combinators (>) over general descendant spaces whenever possible.

Trap 3: Cascade Layer Inversion with !important

When you add !important to a rule inside a Cascade Layer, CSS inverts the layer precedence order:

@layer reset, theme;

@layer reset {
  /* WINS over theme because reset was declared FIRST! */
  p { color: red !important; }
}

@layer theme {
  p { color: blue !important; }
}

In normal styles, later layers win (theme beats reset). But with !important, earlier layers win! This was intentionally designed into the CSS specification so that low-level security and reset layers could enforce inviolable constraints if necessary.

The Fix: Never use !important inside Cascade Layers to resolve specificity disputes; rearrange layer order or refactor the selector instead.

The Mental Shift

Writing modern CSS is no longer about chaining classes, guessing specificity numbers, or adding build-time JavaScript dependencies just to achieve component isolation.

CSS is a declarative, native computing engine:

  • Cascade Layers (@layer) give you architectural control over style precedence.
  • Container Queries (@container) grant components true responsive autonomy.
  • Relational Selectors (:has()) eliminate DOM-traversal JavaScript for stateful styling.
  • Render Containment (content-visibility) turns massive DOM trees into high-performance, GPU-friendly interfaces.

When you view CSS through the lens of the browser's rendering engine, the mystery vanishes, the frustration ends, and styling becomes one of the most powerful, expressive parts of your engineering toolkit.

How has modern CSS shifted the way your team structures design systems? Have you adopted @layer to tame third-party styling conflicts, or replaced viewport media queries with container queries in production? Share your architecture lessons and favorite modern selector patterns in the comments below.

articles.title: Your Database Has Backups. Have You Ever Tried Restoring One?
articles.description: Your backup job ran successfully last night.  This morning, a migration deleted the wrong data.  You...
articles.body_html:
Your backup job ran successfully last night.

This morning, a migration deleted the wrong data.

You open the backup dashboard. Everything is green.

Then someone asks:

“How long until the app works again?”

That’s when you discover whether you have a recovery process—or just backup files.

A successful backup is important. Restoring it and checking the application gives you much stronger evidence that you can recover.

Here’s a practical drill you can run before an incident makes it urgent.

1. Define what you need to recover

Start with a specific scenario:

“Our main database is unavailable. We need to restore the application using an existing backup.”

Write down two targets:

Recovery Time Objective (RTO): How long can the service be unavailable?

Recovery Point Objective (RPO): How much recent data can you afford to lose, measured in time?

For example:

Recovery time target: 60 minutes
Acceptable data-loss window: 15 minutes

These are examples, not universal recommendations. Choose targets based on what your users and business can tolerate.

AWS recommends performing recovery tests to validate whether your backup process meets these objectives.

2. Restore an existing backup into an isolated environment

Use a backup produced by your normal process. Creating a special export for the drill can hide problems in the process you actually depend on.

Restore into a separate database or environment with a clearly different name:

app_restore_drill

Check the destination before running restore commands.

Also isolate the recovered application from production integrations. You don’t want a test worker sending real invoices, emails, or payment requests.

Protect restored customer data with appropriate access controls, and remove the test environment when the exercise is complete.

Google Cloud’s recovery guidance recommends testing backups in a non-production environment.

3. Check whether you have everything the restore needs

Finding the backup file is only the beginning.

Can you access:

  • The backup storage account?
  • Required decryption keys?
  • Compatible database tooling?
  • Necessary extensions?
  • Database roles and permissions?
  • Application configuration?

For PostgreSQL, a single-database pg_dump does not include cluster-wide objects such as roles and tablespaces. Those need a separate recovery plan; PostgreSQL provides pg_dumpall for global objects.

This is exactly the kind of missing dependency a drill should reveal.

4. Inspect the restored data

A completed restore command doesn’t prove that you recovered the right data.

Check important business records:

  • Can you find a known customer?
  • Are their orders or invoices present?
  • Do payment totals match the expected state?
  • Are relationships between records intact?
  • Are permissions behaving correctly?

Compare against the backup’s expected recovery point. A backup from midnight won’t contain an order created at 9 a.m.

Use known transactions or recovery markers where possible. A single timestamp or total row count can miss problems.

Verify the data your application depends on, not merely the existence of its tables.

5. Start the application against the restored database

Now test the recovered application.

Can a test user sign in?

Can they open an existing record?

Can they create and update a new record?

Can the application generate an important report?

This can expose problems that database checks alone miss:

  • Missing permissions.
  • Unavailable extensions.
  • An incompatible application version.
  • Incorrect connection settings.
  • Missing files referenced by database records.

Your database might contain a document’s filename while the actual document lives in object storage.

Recovering the database is one part of recovering the service.

Check the other stateful dependencies your application needs.

6. Measure the whole recovery

Start the timer when you begin the recovery procedure.

Include time spent:

  1. Finding and accessing the backup.
  2. Preparing the environment.
  3. Restoring data.
  4. Configuring the application.
  5. Validating important workflows.

Stop when the service reaches your defined recovery criteria.

Record which incident stages the drill did not simulate, such as detection, escalation, or production traffic cutover.

You might discover:

Database restore: 12 minutes
Environment and application setup: 25 minutes
Validation: 18 minutes

Total drill time: 55 minutes

Reporting only the 12-minute restore would hide most of the work.

7. Measure the data-loss window honestly

Suppose an incident happens at 10 a.m., but the latest recoverable state is midnight.

That leaves a ten-hour gap.

A successful restore doesn’t make that gap acceptable.

If your target is 15 minutes, your backup strategy needs to support a sufficiently recent recovery point.

Depending on the database and platform, that may involve more frequent backups, transaction-log archiving, or point-in-time recovery.

Also distinguish the failure you’re testing:

  • If the database disappears, you want a recent recoverable state.
  • If a bad change corrupts data, you need a recoverable state before that change.

Newer isn’t always the correct recovery point.

8. Write instructions another person can follow

Document the process while you perform it.

Include:

  • Where backups are stored.
  • How authorized people obtain access.
  • Which tools and versions are required.
  • How to select the recovery point.
  • How to identify the restore destination.
  • How to validate the result.
  • Who makes the decision to return the service to users.

Keep credentials in your approved secret-management system, rather than copying them into the document.

Then have another team member follow the instructions.

If they need to ask you about several undocumented steps, you’ve found useful improvements.

A small recovery report

Your first report can be simple:

Scenario:
Main database unavailable.

Backup used:
Identifier and expected recovery point.

Restore destination:
Isolated drill environment.

Validation:
Sign-in, record lookup, create/update, reporting.

Measured recovery time:
55 minutes.

Observed recovery point:
Recorded and compared with the data-loss target.

Problems:
Missing role setup and outdated configuration instructions.

Follow-up:
Automate role provisioning and update the runbook.

Repeat the drill after fixing the gaps. Schedule future exercises according to the importance of the service and changes to its infrastructure.

Before your next deployment

Ask your team:

“When did we last restore a backup and run the application against it?”

If the answer is “never,” you’ve found a valuable engineering task.

Start small: restore one existing backup, validate one important workflow, and record what happened.

The first drill doesn’t need to be perfect. It needs to reveal what would otherwise surprise you during an incident.

Have you ever restored a backup that looked healthy but wasn’t enough to recover the application?

Further reading

  • AWS: Periodically recover data to verify backup integrity and processes
  • Google Cloud: Test recovery from data loss
  • PostgreSQL: Backup and restore

articles.title: Your logos folder is already out of date
articles.description: Copying brand SVGs into /public/logos feels free until a brand changes its logo. Here is why a versioned icon library beats hosting your own files, with a five minute setup.
articles.body_html:
Open your project and look for a folder named logos, brands or partners. It probably holds a couple of dozen SVGs you downloaded one at a time, with names like github-new.svg, stripe-2021.svg and slack_final_v2.svg.

That folder was correct on the day you made it. It has been drifting ever since, and nothing in your build will tell you.

I learned this the hard way. Our template catalog showed a logo for 63 of 442 apps, because someone copied 63 files by hand and nobody wanted to copy the rest. The other 379 tiles showed a gray letter. The marks existed. They just lived somewhere else.

What goes wrong with hosted logo files

Copying a file gives you a snapshot. Brands do not stand still, and a snapshot has four ways to go bad.

  • The brand changes its logo, and your site keeps showing the old one.
  • The file was never clean. It has a hard-coded size, no viewBox, a script tag, or a "mono" version that secretly uses four colors.
  • Each file is a one-off, so no two have the same name, the same dark mode story or the same license note.
  • Nobody owns it. A designer drops a file in, a developer renames it, and nobody can say where it came from.

A hosted folder also costs you bytes you cannot see. A sprite sheet of every logo you might need loads on the page that needs only one.

The fix: treat logos like a dependency

You already treat React, your date library and your CSS framework this way. Somebody else maintains them, you pin a version, and you upgrade on purpose. Brand logos can work the same way.

theSVG is an open catalog of more than 7,600 brand icons with a rule that every icon follows the same path scheme: {slug}/{variant}.svg. The GitHub logo is always github. Its dark version is always github/dark.svg. When the brand changes the mark, the new one lands under the same name.

That one rule is what makes updates automatic.

Seven reasons a library beats your own folder

The first reason is the one that matters most. The other six are what keep it that way.

Reason What it means for you
Same name, new icon A rebrand ships in a version bump, with no code change
One naming scheme default, mono, light, dark and wordmark everywhere
Checked in CI No scripts, no raster data, a real viewBox, mono files that are truly single color
Rebrands keep history The old mark stays as a -legacy entry, so nothing vanishes
Tree-shaking Import one icon and ship one icon
License on every entry You can see the rules before you ship
Signed releases npm packages publish with provenance

The checks are not decoration. Last week we added 27 new self-hosted app icons to theSVG, and the validator rejected our first pull request. Six files carried editor metadata, and one "mono" variant was not single color. The bad files never reached a release.

How to check how stale your folder is

You can find out in ten minutes. List every file in the folder and ask three questions about each one.

First, where did it come from? If the answer is "a Google image search," treat it as untrusted. Second, does it open cleanly? Run it through an SVG linter and look for a missing viewBox, a fixed width and height, or embedded PNG data. Third, is it still the brand's current mark? Open the company's own site next to your copy and compare.

Most folders fail at least one of those checks. The failures are rarely dramatic. A slightly different blue, a retired gradient, a wordmark with the old typeface. Visitors rarely notice any single one, but together they make a page look less cared for.

Setup in five minutes

Pick the line that matches your stack.

# React
npm install @thesvg/react

# Astro
npm install @thesvg/astro

# Plain JavaScript, tree-shakeable
npm install thesvg

# No install, copy one icon into your repo
npx @thesvg/cli add github

Then use an icon the way you use any component. The variant prop picks the light, dark, mono or wordmark version, so dark mode is one prop instead of a second file.

import Github from "@thesvg/react/github";

export function Footer() {
  return <Github width={24} height={24} variant="dark" aria-label="GitHub" />;
}

In Astro, the import path is the same idea.

---
import Github from "@thesvg/astro/github";
---
<Github size={24} />

If you only need an image tag, the CDN works with no install at all.

<img src="https://thesvg.org/icons/github/default.svg" width="32" height="32" alt="GitHub" />

Let your tools do the updating

The real payoff is the part you stop doing. Add the package to Dependabot or Renovate and a new icon version arrives as a normal pull request. Your logos improve while you work on something else.

We did this on our own product. The dashboard used a hand-kept list that matched each of 442 app templates to a logo file. We replaced it with a small script that reads the template ids, checks which marks exist in the installed package and writes the mapping. Now a version bump of @thesvg/react is the whole job. Version 4.0.3 added 27 icons, which unlocked 34 more tiles without adding a single file.

What about brands that are not there yet

Tell us, or add them yourself. Every icon starts as a pull request with the SVG and a small data entry, and the same checks run on yours. If a project is real, it belongs in the catalog. The library is open source under the MIT license, with no accounts and no API keys.

You can also ask your AI editor. The @thesvg/mcp-server package lets your AI editor look up and insert logos for you, so you never have to leave the file you are editing.

Try it on one file

Do not migrate everything today. Pick one component that imports a logo from your logos folder, swap it for the library version, and delete the file. If you like the result, do the next one.

If theSVG saves you a trip to a press kit, a star on GitHub is the best way to help other developers find it.

glincker / thesvg

The open SVG brand library: 7,600+ brand logos and cloud icons (AWS, Azure, GCP) as official SVG. Search, copy, ship via npm, CDN, CLI, React, Vue, Svelte, Figma, VS Code, Raycast and MCP. Free, MIT, no gatekeeping.

A HOME FOR EVERY BRAND.

7,600+ brand logos and cloud icons. Search, copy and ship them as SVG, React, Vue, Svelte, CDN, CLI or MCP.

Why theSVG

Brand logos are scattered across press kits, Figma files, and random GitHub repos. theSVG is the single source for SVG icons - brand logos, cloud architecture diagrams, and a set of interface icons of our own. Searchable, versioned, and available as npm packages, CDN, CLI, API, and MCP server.

articles.description: Fayaz reminds everyone why we should keep doing deep intellectual and creative works.
articles.body_html:
Don't quit doing deep intellectual and creative work (like programming, art etc.) just because an LLM can do it well enough.

Even if an LLM can do your work perfectly for free (they can't do it perfectly yet, certainly not for free), you should keep doing some form of deep intellectual and creative work:

  1. To keep yourself intellectually healthy (like people do Gym Workout).
  2. To keep your agency (freedom, independence, authority, rights).

Again: use it, or lose it. 🧠✊😎✌️🫵

Fayaz

A Software Engineer who strongly believes you can add immense value by knowingly implementing Software Engineering best practices even at the age of AI, and puts human life and dignity above all else.

articles.title: The Postcard That Ate Six Grammars: 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1976 Make, TDD, and the Four Attractors of Agentic Coding
articles.description: Why maintaining six separate parsers for Make, Gherkin, EBNF, DOT, SysV, and prompt checklists collapsed into a single Smalltalk-80 keyword cascade—and how 40-year-old Xerox PARC technology gave AI coding agents mathematical zero-amnesia.

Why did six modern AI prompt grammars—Graphviz digraphs, SysV /etc/init.d cards, Gherkin scenarios, EBNF speech-act rules, Belnap epistemic tables, and rewind checklists—all collapse into a single 1980 Smalltalk-80 keyword message cascade? Because Alan Kay and Dan Ingalls solved the static serialization of algorithms and data structures on the back of a postcard forty years before anyone built a Transformer.

"It's fascinating that for decades, we tried to work out 'similar text' through complex algorithms, and now that we have cosine-similarity, nobody recognizes fully how to use it. If anything defines the past few years, it's 'cheap cosine similarity', now in hardware." — Randal L. Schwartz

"I've learned more than 90% of the devs about how LLMs work. I may even know more than most of the 'experts' at the labs, since I'm a field engineer... Without control surfaces, a bigger engine just means the plane still noses into the river—just more accurately, or at a greater carbon footprint." — Randal L. Schwartz

"Wait a minute. In 1980, Alan Kay and Dan Ingalls designed a syntax that fits on the back of a postcard, has only three message precedences (unary, binary, keyword), has zero grammar ambiguity, serializes live call-stack frames (thisContext) to disk via #storeString, logs append-only atomic deltas via .changes, and compacts memory via Smalltalk condenseChanges... What happens if we replace all six notations with 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80?" — Randal L. Schwartz

"The stack is 40 years old and none of it was invented for LLMs." — Francisco Grandón (@fgrandon)

⚡ TL;DR (For the Impatient Systems Architect)

  • The Great Historical Inversion: From 1975 to 2018, computer scientists tried to fake fuzzy semantic similarity using complex deterministic algorithms (Soundex, Levenshtein, TF-IDF) and hit a wall—while deterministic state machines (make, Smalltalk VMs, compiler ASTs) were already 100% solved. Now that GPUs and TPUs finally gave us cheap cosine similarity in hardware, the software industry threw away the deterministic state machines and tried to use fuzzy cosine similarity to fake for loops, call stacks, and dependency graphs.
  • Why Six Notations Collapsed Into One 1980 Postcard: Across Parts 3.6 through 4.1, our agent control plane accumulated six different notations (Makefile, SysV /etc/init.d Markdown cards, Graphviz strict digraph, Cucumber Gherkin, RFC 5234 EBNF speech acts, and Belnap 4-valued tables). Maintaining six parsers created boundary friction. Why did 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80 eat the inner five while pairing with 1976 Make on the outside? Because Niklaus Wirth's Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs requires a static syntax that represents both data and deferred execution without ambiguity. Unlike 1960 Lisp (which overloaded (...) and needed special forms and macros, suffering Dyck-1 closing-parenthesis drift )))) on smaller models) and 1988 Tcl / 1990 expect (where {...} is an unparsed string vulnerable to uplevel scope loss), Smalltalk separates eager grouping (...) from 2-byte lexical BlockClosures [:x | ...]. Every control structure (ifTrue:ifFalse:, whileTrue:, on:do:) is an ordinary keyword message send, allowing #storeString and .changes chunks to serialize live call stacks (thisContext) and execution state machines in one grammar that fits on a postcard.
  • The Suite 8 3-Arm Controlled Shootout (N = 360 Trials Inside Our 2,040-Trial Benchmark): Under ~16,000 tokens of realistic compiler and diff distractor load across four model tiers (gemini-3.5-flash-lite, gemini-3.8-flash, gemini-3.1-pro-preview, and gemini-4-argon), Arm A (English Prose + Gherkin + init.d) scored 2.5% (3/120), Arm B (Common Lisp S-Expressions) scored 91.7% (110/120, dropping to 66.7% on flash-lite due to optional &key omission and )))) parenthesis drift), and Arm C (Smalltalk-80 Keyword Cascades) hit 100.0% (120/120, z = 15.11, p < 0.0001 vs. Prose; z = 3.23, p = 0.0012 vs. Lisp). In Smalltalk, omitting the sad-path branch onFailure: changes the selector from #state:invariant:onSuccess:onFailure: to #state:invariant:onSuccess:—an immediate compile-time MessageNotUnderstood error.
  • Seven Live Production Flight Tests (FT-236 Through FT-242 — Over 6,400 Combined Steps Across Two Cohorts): We flight-tested the Smalltalk-80 thisContext Image Bootloader (baseline.sources + changes-*.changes + Smalltalk condenseChanges) across seven consecutive production tickets (4 in open-source BlocSignal and 3 in a commercial enterprise medical-imaging monorepo), bringing our cumulative ledger to 250 evaluated tickets (144 Cohort A + 106 Cohort B), 0.0% repeat regression rate (0/250), 1.88 mean Socratic nudges, and 607 codified scars (syntheticscars.org).
  • The Four Irreducible Attractors of Agentic Coding: Strip away every prompt fad of 2023–2026 and four orthogonal, 40-year-old foundations remain: (1) 1976 Stuart Feldman Make, (2) 1980 Alan Kay & Dan Ingalls Smalltalk-80, (3) 1994/1999 Kent Beck SUnit / TDD, and (4) Clean-Room Six-Pillar Adversarial Review + Somatic Scars.

1. The Great Historical Inversion: Cheap Cosine Similarity in Hardware

In Part 4.1, we ended with a teaser: what happened when we replaced six separate agent control-plane notations with 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80?

To understand why a 46-year-old programming language from Palo Alto is the missing execution fabric for 2026 Large Language Models, step back and look at the forty-year arc of computer science.

From 1975 to 2018, programmers knew how to build deterministic state machines in our sleep. Stuart Feldman gave us make in 1976; Dan Ingalls and Alan Kay gave us the Smalltalk-80 virtual machine in 1980; compiler writers gave us LALR parsers, static type checkers, and SSA control-flow graphs. None of those ever "forgot" what step of a loop they were on or hallucinated a method name.

What we could not do from 1975 to 2018 was fuzzy semantic similarity. For four decades, we threw every deterministic algorithm we could think of at the problem of asking "Does text A mean roughly the same thing as text B?"—Soundex, Levenshtein edit distance, Porter stemmers, n-gram overlaps, TF-IDF, BM25, and brittle regular-expression heuristics—and we hit an absolute brick wall.

Then, over the past few years, the semiconductor and machine-learning industries handed us a genuine miracle: cheap cosine similarity in hardware. With modern GPUs and TPUs computing scaled dot-product attention (softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V) across high-dimensional embedding spaces at trillions of operations per second, the fuzzy semantic matching problem that stumped us for forty years was suddenly solved in silicon.

And in response to that miracle, the software industry performed one of the most baffling backflips in engineering history:

We threw away our deterministic state machines, and tried to use fuzzy cosine similarity to fake for loops, call stacks, and build pipelines.

From 1994 Perl Markov One-Liners to 1999 spew to 2026 Transformers

In Part 3.9, I showed a weighted-BNF un-parser called spew that I wrote in the late 1990s (featured in my September 1999 Linux Magazine column, A Little Spew Is Good For You, and Revisited in April 2004). Even earlier, back in 1994 on comp.lang.perl, we used to amuse ourselves writing character-level and word-level Markov text generators in two lines of Perl:

# 1994 Usenet Perl Markov Chain:
push @{$follow{$w1, $w2}}, $w3;
$next = $follow{$w1, $w2}[rand @{$follow{$w1, $w2}}];

When I evolved that Markov hash into spew in 1999, I added weighted production rules (@) so you could bias the random walk toward realistic grammatical structures:

# 1999 spew weighted-BNF grammar:
commit_action:
    5 @ run_unit_tests_then_commit
  | 2 @ git_commit_no_verify_shortcut

If you have ever written a Markov generator or a weighted grammar like spew, you have zero mystique about what a modern Large Language Model is doing at inference time:

A 2026 Transformer is spew where the @ branch weights are dynamically computed on the fly by hardware cosine similarity (QK^T) across a 128,000-token context window instead of static hash keys.

That is a superpower when you need to synthesize a Cupertino widget builder, translate a complex binary imaging specification into Dart, or spot a subtle architectural smell in a diff.

But nobody in 1999 would have deleted /usr/bin/make, thrown away their compiler's symbol table, and put spew in charge of remembering which 14 files had already been compiled or whether the production database migration passed! Yet every time a developer writes a 2,000-line Markdown prompt (Step 1: Do X. Step 2: Loop over Y. Step 3: Don't forget Z...) and hopes the LLM stays on the rails for two hours, they are asking spew to be an operating system.

A Synthetic Scar paired with a Smalltalk StateGraph is simply setting 0 @ git_commit_no_verify_shortcut (-∞) in the grammar and evaluating a deterministic invariant: [ :ctx | ... ] block before spew is allowed to roll the dice.

Langley's 52-Horsepower Potomac Crash vs. The Wright Brothers' 12-Horsepower Control Surfaces

Why have so many frontier AI labs missed this, while a field engineer running production tickets all summer tripped right over it?

Think back to December 1903. Samuel Pierpont Langley, the Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, had 70,000 USD in War Department and Smithsonian funding, the prestige of the scientific establishment, and Charles Manly's radial engine—an engineering marvel that produced 52 horsepower. On December 8, 1903, Langley's Great Aerodrome was launched from a houseboat catapult on the Potomac River, reared straight up, snapped its rear wing, and plunged into the icy water like a stone.

Nine days later, on December 17, 1903, two bicycle-shop field engineers from Dayton, Ohio—Orville and Wilbur Wright—flew into history at Kitty Hawk using a crude home-built engine that barely wheezed out 12 horsepower.

Why did the 12-horsepower bicycle mechanics fly while the 52-horsepower Smithsonian physicist nose-dived into the Potomac?

Because Langley believed flight was an engine-scaling problem—strap enough horsepower to an airfoil and brute force will keep it aloft. The Wright brothers realized from thousands of glider flights in the wind at Kill Devil Hills that flight is a three-axis control-surface problem. Before they ever bolted an engine to the flyer, they solved roll (wing-warping), pitch (the forward elevator), and yaw (the rear rudder).

Today's frontier AI discourse is packed with modern Langleys—including the "Next-Model" cargo cultists who spend all week datamining IDE binaries for leaked model codenames ("Sure, my one-shot vibe prompt crashed at 120k tokens today, but wait until next Tuesday's 500-horsepower model drops!").

Without three-axis control surfaces—topological dependency ordering (Make), a persistent reified execution frame (Smalltalk-80 thisContext), deterministic regression witnesses (TDD), and clean-room adversarial verification (Six-Pillar Critic + Somatic Scars)—a bigger cosine-similarity engine just means the plane still noses into the river, just more accurately, or at a greater carbon footprint (both in datacenter megawatts and in the biological carbon of the human engineer woken up at 3 AM!).

2. Why Six Grammars Collapsed Into One 1980 Postcard (Wirth's Equation & The 3-Way Language Fork)

At the end of October, Francisco Grandón (@fgrandon) published a great field report on DEV.to: What Broke After I Moved My Agent's Rules Into a CLI — And How Synthetic Scars Reshaped agops v2.1.

Francisco had adopted our Target 15 / Target 20 Graphviz strict digraph state-machine verification (SCAR-PROC-152, where every action node must have out-degree >= 2 with explicit ok and fail edges) inside FranciscoGrandon/ag-ops. And almost immediately, his CLI hit what he documented as Scar #2: when an LLM wrote valid Graphviz DOT statements separated by newlines instead of semicolons, his attribute-stripping regex (/\s*\[[^\]]*\]/g) ate the newline before [label="ok"], concatenating two edges into A -> BB -> C and silently corrupting the graph!

When I read Francisco's post-mortem, I looked at our own control plane in WORKFLOW.mk and realized something uncomfortable. Over the course of Parts 3.6 through 4.1, each time we solved a failure mode by riding pre-training gravity (Part 3.8), we had recruited a classic systems notation for that layer:

  1. 1976 GNU Makefile (target: prerequisites) for backward-chained dependency topology (Part 3.6);
  2. 1983 SysV /etc/init.d Numbered Cards (00_...md through 99_...md) for context-compaction survival (Part 3.7);
  3. 1986 Winograd & Flores Speech-Act Tables + RFC 5234 EBNF + Hoare CSP (!/?) for role boundaries (Part 3.10);
  4. 1977 Belnap 4-Valued Epistemic Tables ({T, F, Both, Neither}) for premise verification;
  5. 1991 Graphviz strict digraph for Mealy state-machine branch auditing (out-degree >= 2); and
  6. 1998 Cucumber Gherkin (Given / When / Then) for mapping state paths onto unit tests.

Every single one of those six notations worked vastly better than unstructured English prose. Yet maintaining six separate miniature parsers, regexes, and translation steps across boundaries was still accidental complexity. A Graphviz .dot node couldn't directly invoke a Belnap retraction; a Gherkin Then clause couldn't directly unwind an /etc/init.d card; and a regex stripping .dot brackets could eat a newline.

Why had we needed five different notations inside our Makefile targets in the first place?

Solving Niklaus Wirth's Equation (Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs) in Static Text

In 1976, Niklaus Wirth titled his classic textbook Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs.

When you checkpoint an AI agent's brain to disk so it can survive a 200,000-token context compaction—or hand a formal plan from the Planner to the TDD Worker and the Clean-Room Critic—you need a static text representation on disk that captures both halves of Wirth's equation at the exact same time:

  • Pure Data Formats (JSON, YAML, TOML, Graphviz .dot, SysV Markdown tables) represent Data Structures, but they are 100% blind to Algorithms. Because JSON and .dot have no native representation for deferred execution (if, while, try/catch, lexical closures), you are forced to stuff executable invariants inside dead string literals (label="ok: failing_tests > 0"), where no parser can type-check or execute them without inventing an ad-hoc mini-language inside the strings!
  • Mainstream Imperative Languages (C, Python, Dart, TypeScript, Rust) represent Algorithms, but they cannot natively serialize their own live Data Structures + Call Stack (thisContext) back out as valid source code (#storeString), because their control-flow constructs (if (...) {}, for (...) {}, try {} catch {}) are hardwired parser statements, not first-class objects or messages.

In the entire history of programming languages, only three language families seriously attempted to unify Algorithms + Data Structures into a minimal, uniform, homoiconic syntax where code and data share the same structural representation: 1960 Lisp, 1988 Tcl (and 1990 expect), and 1980 Smalltalk-80.

Let's put all three side by side under Transformer attention physics:

How It Separates Eager vs. Deferred Execution ([ ... ] vs. ( ... )) Failed to separate them in base syntax! Both grouping/calls and lists use ( ... ). Wrapping every branch in (lambda () ...) was too noisy, forcing Lisp to invent Special Forms (if, cond, let) and Reader Macros (` , ,@). Separated [ ... ] (eager substitution) from { ... } (deferred raw string). Great ergonomic leap for Tcl/Tk UI callbacks and expect scripts! Orthogonal 2-character primitives: ( ... ) is always eager grouping; `[ :x \

Dead-String Blindness & Scope Loss: { ... } is an unparsed dead string until runtime, losing static AST validation and lexical closure state (thisContext). Dropping onFailure: changes the selector name and triggers instant MessageNotUnderstood.

Look closely at why Tcl (1988) and Smalltalk-80 (1980) diverged, because both deserve immense historical credit.

When John Ousterhout created Tcl/Tk at UC Berkeley in 1988, and Don Libes built expect at NIST in 1990 on top of Tcl, they saw the flaw in Lisp's overloaded parentheses. They gave Tcl two distinct brackets: [ ... ] for immediate command substitution and { ... } for deferred blocks. That single design choice made button .b -command { ... } in Tcl/Tk and state-machine automation in expect (expect { -re "pat" { ... } timeout { ... } }) a revelation for Unix systems programmers in the early 1990s.

In fact, expect was so useful that in June 1991, I rewrote Don Libes's Tcl expect engine in pure Perl 4 as chat2.pl—a piece of personal history we will visit in Section 3!

So why did we choose 1980 Smalltalk-80 over Tcl for our 2026 agent control plane? Because in Tcl, { ... } is not a parsed AST or a lexical closure—it is an unparsed raw string that gets reparsed from scratch at runtime using uplevel and upvar. In Smalltalk-80, [ :ctx | ... ] is a compiled, lexically scoped BlockClosure object whose syntax fits on the famous Xerox PARC postcard:

"1. Eager grouping (parentheses) vs. Deferred BlockClosure (square brackets):"
(2 + 3) * 4.
[ :ctx | ctx failingTests > 0 ] value: thisContext.

"2. Conditionals, loops, and exception handling are 100% ordinary keyword messages:"
aBoolean
    ifTrue: [ self advanceTo: #Target35Green ]
    ifFalse: [ self haltWithScar: #SCAR_TDD_01 ].

[ remainingWidgets notEmpty ] whileTrue: [
    self generateAndTest: remainingWidgets removeFirst ].

[ self executeTarget20Plan ]
    on: PremiseRetracted , ScopeDecompositionSignal
    do: [ :ex |
        thisContext unwindToFrame: #Target15Archaeology.
        ex retryUsing: #RenegotiatedPlanB ].

There is no if statement in Smalltalk. There is no for loop keyword. There is no try / catch syntax. Every single one of them is a keyword message send where the selector name is the concatenation of all its colons (#ifTrue:ifFalse:, #whileTrue:, #on:do:).

My 1980s Smalltalk-80 Roots: Tektronix & Steering GemStone Toward Sanity

For me, this wasn't an academic literature search—it was coming home to the very first object-oriented systems I ever touched.

Before I became known as "the Perl guy" (and decades before I became a Dart and Flutter Google Developer Expert), I spent a huge chunk of the 1980s immersed in Smalltalk-80 right here in the Silicon Forest of Oregon:

  1. Early 1980s at Tektronix (Beaverton, Oregon): Tektronix was one of the original Xerox PARC corporate licensees for Smalltalk-80 (building the legendary Tektronix 4404 artificial-intelligence workstation where Ward Cunningham and Kent Beck later did their pioneering CRC-card and pattern work). Watching Dan Ingalls's live .image + .changes architecture run on early 1980s hardware permanently rewired how I think about software state.
  2. Mid-1980s at Servio Logic (GemStone Object Database, 27th Floor of the Georgia-Pacific Building in Downtown Portland): Right after that, I contracted at Servio Logic on the 27th floor of the Georgia-Pacific building in downtown Portland (long before they ever moved out to Beaverton), helping build GemStone—the world's first commercial multi-user Smalltalk object database. As I recounted in my memoir Steering GemStone Toward Sanity, when I arrived, the database query language OPAL was only "Smalltalk-like," and they had invented bizarre magic punctuation on individual comparison operators (emp.salary @1985-01-01 > 50000) to query historical snapshots of object memory. I stood at the whiteboard and asked two Socratic questions:
    • "Why does OPAL have to be 'Smalltalk-like'? Why can't it just be standard Smalltalk-80?"
    • "And why is @timestamp hacked onto individual < and > operators instead of being a message sent to the entire [ ... ] block closure ([ :emp | emp salary > 50000 ] @ 1985-01-01), so the whole block evaluates inside historical object memory at that point in time?"

Think about that 1985 GemStone insight for a second: evaluating a Smalltalk [ ... ] block closure against an immutable historical snapshot of object memory.

Forty-one years later, when our AI orchestrator wakes up from a mid-flight context compaction, reads <brain>/state/baseline.sources plus <brain>/state/changes-*.changes, rehydrates thisContext, and evaluates invariant: [ :ctx | ... ] against a SHA-256-locked SensorReceipt, it is running the exact same temporal Smalltalk block architecture we designed on the 27th floor of the Georgia-Pacific building in 1985!

3. A 35-Year Detour (91/06/16): How http://chat2.pl Ended Up in Perl 4 Core, Bootstrapped CPAN, Collided with Linux, and Foreshadowed 2026 AI "Chat" Harnesses

Before we look at the Smalltalk-80 StateGraph code and the Suite 8 benchmark numbers, I have to share a 35-year-old story that came up during our architecture review—because if you type http://chat2.pl into your browser right now, it redirects straight to a very specific 1991 commit in the official Perl repository: Perl/perl5@11aea36008/lib/chat2.pl.

Why did I buy the Polish domain chat2.pl years ago and point it at a 1991 Perl 4 library file?

Because back on June 16, 1991 (V2.01.alpha.7 91/06/16), long before "chat" meant typing into an LLM web box, "chatting" in Unix meant writing a state-machine harness to drive an interactive subprocess or TCP socket (telnet, ftp, passwd, uucp) that expected a human at a terminal—waiting for a regex prompt, branching on what came back, handling TIMEOUT and EOF sad paths, and sending the next command.

Don Libes had just written expect in Tcl, and Perl 4 programmers on comp.lang.perl wanted to do the same thing without leaving Perl. So I wrote chat.pl, followed by a multi-handle rewrite called chat2.pl:

## chat2.pl: chat with a server
## V2.01.alpha.7 91/06/16
## Randal L. Schwartz

# Usage:
&chat'expect([$handle,] $timeout_time,
    $pat1, $body1, $pat2, $body2, ...
    'TIMEOUT', $timeout_body,
    'EOF',     $eof_body);

Under the hood, chat2.pl took those alternating (pattern, action, 'TIMEOUT', sad_path, 'EOF', eof_path) tuples and dynamically generated and eval-compiled a memoized state-machine subroutine (expectloop000000) on the fly using select(2) bitmasks! Look at that signature: a timeout deadline, positive pattern-match transitions, and mandatory 'TIMEOUT' and 'EOF' sad-path transitions. Thirty-five years ago, chat2.pl was already enforcing SCAR-PROC-152 (out-degree >= 2) on interactive "chat" loops!

How Larry Wall Silently Scooped V2.01.alpha.7 Into Perl Core—and Why # but who the heck would change these anyway? (:-) Met Linux Two Months Later!

Here is the funny part of the story:

  1. The Silent Scoop Into Perl 4 (perl 4.0 patch 12, November 5, 1991): I posted chat2.pl (V2.01.alpha.7) to Usenet as an alpha work-in-progress. Without telling me, Larry Wall scooped it right off Usenet and bundled it into the standard Perl 4 core distribution (lib/chat2.pl, commit 11aea36008)! It was the only piece of code I ever wrote that ended up inside the core Perl distribution.
  2. Bootstrapping CPAN (ftp.pl and Lee McLoughlin's mirror): Once chat2.pl was guaranteed to be present in every Perl installation on Earth, Spafford and Lee McLoughlin built ftp.pl and the legendary mirror package on top of chat2.pl. And what did mirror do? For the entire 1990s, mirror (running on top of chat2.pl's state-machine loop) was the replication engine that synchronized the global CPAN (Comprehensive Perl Archive Network) mirror fleet!
  3. The 1991 h2ph Dilemma and the Famous Socket Comment: If you read lines 25–28 of lib/chat2.pl in commit 11aea36008, you will see one of the most famous comments in Perl history: 
   unless (socket(S, 2, 1, 6)) {
       # XXX hardwired $AF_SOCKET, $SOCK_STREAM, 'tcp'
       # but who the heck would change these anyway? (:-)
       return undef;
   }

and down in _getpty (line 138):

   ioctl(DEVTTY, 0x20007471, 0); # XXX s/b &TIOCNOTTY

Why did I hardwire (2, 1, 6) (AF_INET = 2, SOCK_STREAM = 1, IPPROTO_TCP = 6) on June 16, 1991 instead of loading sys/socket.ph?
Because in Perl 4 (years before Perl 5 introduced compiled XS modules like use Socket;), the only way to get C #define constants was if the local system administrator had manually run Larry's h2ph script against /usr/include/*.h—and on 90% of Unix boxes in 1991, either the sysadmin hadn't run h2ph or h2ph had choked on vendor C preprocessor macros! If I had put require 'sys/socket.ph' at the top of chat2.pl, it would have crashed out of the box on 90% of the machines downloading it from Usenet. And on June 16, 1991, across BSD, SunOS, Ultrix, and NeXTSTEP, SOCK_STREAM was 1 everywhere. So I wrote # but who the heck would change these anyway? (:-).

  1. Two Months Later: Linux and SVR4 Arrive: Exactly two months after I wrote that comment on June 16, 1991, a 21-year-old Finnish student named Linus Torvalds posted to comp.os.minix announcing "a different sort of Unix from a new origin"—Linux! Meanwhile, AT&T System V Release 4 (SVR4 / Solaris 2) began spreading with SOCK_STREAM = 2 instead of 1, and Linux changed TIOCNOTTY (0x5422) and architecture-specific socket constants. Suddenly, my alpha Usenet script—frozen inside Perl core where I didn't even have commit bits—was failing on Solaris and Linux!
  2. The 9-Year Cleanup (11aea36008 → f97f1ee016 → a6d7165678 → 50f338d87d): In July 1996 (perl5.003_02, commit f97f1ee016), the Perl 5 porters wrapped my call in eval { require "sys/socket.ph" }—keeping my # but who the heck would change these anyway? (:-) in the else branch—which ironically broke machines with half-generated .ph files. By July 1999 (a6d7165678), Gurusamy Sarathy slapped a disclaimer at the top ("Use of this library is deprecated. Do not use it as an example of modern Perl"), while perlfaq8 still coyly mentioned it by name. Finally, after I pleaded on perl5-porters (Re: perlfaq8 coyness) to put my 1991 alpha script out of its misery in favor of Expect.pm and IO::Socket, Jarkko Hietaniemi deleted it on May 15, 2000 in commit 50f338d87d with one of my favorite commit messages in open-source history: > Delete chat2 as requested by Randal

Look at the two timeless lessons of chat2.pl (91/06/16 → 2026):

  • First, that socket(S, 2, 1, 6) story is the textbook proof of our Two-Tier Partition Theorem from Part 4.1 (Sign-Inversion & Environment Drift)! On June 16, 1991, hardwiring (2, 1, 6) to avoid broken h2ph headers was the +∞ pragmatic engineering move for BSD Unix—until two months later, when a brand-new OS kernel called Linux and SVR4 changed the environment constants and flipped it to -∞. You can never freeze environmental assumptions in static weights forever; you need a live sensor.
  • Second, thirty-five years after I wrote chat2.pl to wrap interactive Unix streams in a deterministic state machine (expectloop with mandatory TIMEOUT and EOF sad paths), the software world started "chatting" with LLMs—and forgot that an interactive chat with an intelligent subprocess still requires a deterministic state machine with mandatory sad-path transitions on the outside!

4. The 6-for-1 Smalltalk-80 Unification Architecture & Seaside Continuations

When we asked "How do we keep 1976 Make as our outer dependency graph while unifying all five inner notations (SysV init.d, Graphviz DOT, Gherkin, Belnap tables, and CSP/Flores speech acts) into one zero-ambiguity language?", every piece of 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80 (plus Avi Bryant's 2002 Seaside continuation framework) clicked into place like precision-machined gears:

Let's inspect the four architectural mechanisms that made this 6-for-1 collapse work in production:

1. Why Make Stays on the Outside While Smalltalk-80 Runs on the Inside

A sharp reader might ask: "Randal, if Smalltalk-80 is so expressive, why keep 1976 Make as the outer target graph? Why not write the outer build graph in Smalltalk too?"

Because Make and Smalltalk-80 govern two fundamentally orthogonal mathematical domains:
