articles.title: I Drained a List From the Front. It Shifted Five Billion Elements.
articles.description: I used a List as a FIFO queue and drained it with RemoveAt(0). Then I measured why a loop that just sums numbers went quadratic, and found the fix had nothing to do with swapping in a Queue.
articles.body_html:
I had a List<int> standing in for a work queue. Jobs went on the back, and a loop pulled them off the front one at a time: read list[0], list.RemoveAt(0), do the work, repeat until the list was empty. It worked. It also crawled once the backlog got into the tens of thousands, and I couldn't see why a loop that just sums numbers would care how many numbers there were in a way that wasn't linear.

So I did the thing I always end up doing. I counted.

RemoveAt(0) moves everything else down

A List<T> is an array with a count on top. When you remove the item at index 0, every element after it has to slide down one slot to close the gap. Remove the front of a 100,000-item list and that's 99,999 elements copied. Do it again and it's 99,998. Keep going until the list is empty and you've shifted the sum of every number from 99,999 down to zero.

That sum is n * (n - 1) / 2, which is the quadratic you were trying not to write.

foreach (int n in new[] { 25_000, 50_000, 100_000 })
{
    long shifts = (long)n * (n - 1) / 2;
    Console.WriteLine($"n = {n,7:N0}  ->  {shifts,18:N0} element shifts");
}

n =  25,000  ->         312,487,500 element shifts
n =  50,000  ->       1,249,975,000 element shifts
n = 100,000  ->       4,999,950,000 element shifts

Five billion element moves to empty a list of a hundred thousand ints. The work I actually cared about was adding up a hundred thousand numbers. Everything else was the list closing gaps I'd just opened.

Putting a clock on it

I measured it the way I measure everything: fill a fresh collection, drain it, sum what comes out so nothing gets optimized away, best of five runs. This isn't a lab, it's a container, so I'm not going to pretend the millisecond counts are anything but rough. The shape is the point.

static long DrainWithListRemoveAt(int[] source)
{
    var list = new List<int>(source);
    long sum = 0;
    while (list.Count > 0)
    {
        int job = list[0];
        list.RemoveAt(0);        // shifts every remaining element down one
        sum += job;
    }
    return sum;
}

static long DrainWithQueue(int[] source)
{
    var queue = new Queue<int>(source);
    long sum = 0;
    while (queue.Count > 0)
        sum += queue.Dequeue();  // no shifting
    return sum;
}

n =  25,000
    List.RemoveAt(0)          315.04 ms
    Queue<int>.Dequeue()        0.07 ms

n =  50,000
    List.RemoveAt(0)         1284.42 ms
    Queue<int>.Dequeue()        0.13 ms

n = 100,000
    List.RemoveAt(0)         5193.70 ms
    Queue<int>.Dequeue()        0.14 ms

Double the size and the list takes roughly four times as long. That four-times-for-double is the signature of an O(n²) loop, and it's exactly what the shift count predicted. The Queue barely moves off zero because dequeuing is just bumping a head index.

I left the "list is 30,000x faster" line out on purpose. That ratio is meaningless. You're comparing something quadratic to something linear, so the gap keeps widening with no natural number at the end of it. The honest read is simpler: one of these grows with the square of your backlog and the other doesn't.

It isn't really a List problem

Here's the part that made me put the article together instead of just swapping in a Queue and moving on. I ran the same List<int>, with the same number of items, but pulled from the back instead of the front.

static long DrainFromEnd(int[] source)
{
    var list = new List<int>(source);
    long sum = 0;
    while (list.Count > 0)
    {
        int job = list[^1];
        list.RemoveAt(list.Count - 1);  // last slot, nothing after it to shift
        sum += job;
    }
    return sum;
}

n = 100,000
    List.RemoveAt(0)         5193.70 ms
    List.RemoveAt(Count-1)      0.11 ms
    Queue<int>.Dequeue()        0.14 ms

Same list, same count, and it's right there with the Queue. RemoveAt(Count - 1) drops the last slot, and there's nothing behind it to move, so each removal is O(1). The five seconds was never about List<T> being slow. It was about repeatedly removing from the one position that forces a full shift.

That distinction matters because the fix depends on what you actually need. If order is up to you, draining from the end costs nothing and you keep your list. If you genuinely need first-in-first-out, Queue<T> is the type that was built for it, and it reads better than a list pretending to be one. Reaching for LinkedList<T> here is usually the wrong instinct, by the way; it gives you cheap removal but spends an allocation per node and wrecks cache locality, and for a plain FIFO it loses to Queue<T> on nearly everything.

And to be fair to RemoveAt(0): if your list is small, or you're pulling off the front once in a blue moon, none of this registers. A ten-item list doesn't care. The trap is specifically the loop that drains a big collection from the front, because that's where the per-call shift turns into a per-run square. I only noticed because the backlog grew past the size where I'd ever tested it.

The rule I walked away with: if a loop removes from the front of a list every iteration, that loop is quadratic, and the front is the problem, not the list.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. The harness is nothing clever: warm up once so the JIT has done its work, take the best of five, and BuildJobs just fills an array so each int stands in for a small unit of work.

int[] sizes = [25_000, 50_000, 100_000];
foreach (int n in sizes)
{
    int[] source = BuildJobs(n);
    (double listMs, _) = BestOf(5, () => DrainWithListRemoveAt(source));
    (double endMs, _)  = BestOf(5, () => DrainFromEnd(source));
    (double queueMs, _) = BestOf(5, () => DrainWithQueue(source));
    Console.WriteLine($"n={n,7:N0}  front {listMs,8:F2}ms  end {endMs,6:F2}ms  queue {queueMs,6:F2}ms");
}

static int[] BuildJobs(int n)
{
    var jobs = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) jobs[i] = i & 1023;
    return jobs;
}

static (double ms, long result) BestOf(int runs, Func<long> body)
{
    body();                              // warm up / JIT
    double best = double.MaxValue;
    long result = 0;
    var sw = new System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch();
    for (int i = 0; i < runs; i++)
    {
        sw.Restart();
        result = body();
        sw.Stop();
        best = Math.Min(best, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }
    return (best, result);
}

Ever get bitten by a collection doing exactly what you asked instead of what you meant? I'd like to hear it.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: Your API Errors Shouldn't Be a Guessing Game
articles.description: Imagine you're building a frontend application and an API request fails.  The backend returns:    {  ...
articles.body_html:
Imagine you're building a frontend application and an API request fails.

The backend returns:

{
  "message": "Something went wrong"
}

Great. But what went wrong?

Was it a validation error? A missing resource? A permission issue? Or something else?

Now the frontend has to guess what happened.

There's a better way to handle API errors, and it's already standardized.

The Problem With API Errors

Different APIs often return errors in different formats.

One endpoint returns:

{
  "error": "Invalid email"
}

Another returns:

{
  "message": "User not found",
  "code": 404
}

And another might accidentally expose an internal database error.

This makes frontend development harder because every endpoint needs different error-handling logic.

What if every API followed the same error structure?

Meet Problem Details

RFC 7807 introduced a standard format called Problem Details for HTTP APIs.

It was later replaced by RFC 9457, which is the current standard.

The idea is simple: return errors in a consistent, predictable format.

Here's an example:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "Insufficient Funds",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Your balance is $40, but the total is $55.",
  "instance": "/checkouts/123"
}

Much better, right?

Every field has a purpose:

  • type: Identifies the kind of error.
  • title: A short description of the problem.
  • status: The HTTP status code.
  • detail: Explains what happened in this request.
  • instance: Identifies the specific occurrence of the problem.

The API should also return the appropriate HTTP status code and this content type:

Content-Type: application/problem+json

Now the frontend knows what kind of problem occurred without guessing from random messages.

What About Form Validation?

This is where it gets even more useful.

Imagine a registration form with invalid inputs.

Your API could return:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/validation",
  "title": "Validation Failed",
  "status": 422,
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "email",
      "message": "Invalid email address"
    },
    {
      "field": "password",
      "message": "Must contain at least 8 characters"
    }
  ]
}

The errors array is a custom extension, not a required field in the standard.

Now the frontend can display each error beside the correct input.

No need to parse random error strings.

Handling Errors in JavaScript

Here's a simple example using fetch:

const response = await fetch("/api/register", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(formData)
});

if (!response.ok) {
  const problem = await response.json();

  if (problem.type === "https://api.example.com/problems/validation") {
    console.log(problem.errors);
  } else {
    console.error(problem.title);
  }
}

In a real application, you should also handle network failures and responses that don't contain valid JSON.

The important part is that your frontend can rely on documented error types instead of matching message strings.

A Few Things Worth Remembering

Using Problem Details doesn't automatically solve every error-handling problem.

You still need to follow a few good practices:

  • Never expose stack traces, SQL queries, or internal secrets.
  • Keep error types stable so frontend code doesn't break.
  • Use appropriate HTTP status codes.
  • Use safe, user-friendly messages where appropriate.
  • Add a request ID when useful for debugging and support.

For localization, frontend applications can map stable error types to translated messages instead of relying on English error descriptions.

Final Thoughts

A good API isn't just about returning successful responses.

It's also about explaining failures clearly.

RFC 9457 gives us a standard way to do that.

No random error structures. No guessing from message strings. Just predictable errors that both frontend and backend developers can understand.

And the best part?

You don't need a new library or framework to get started. Just a consistent error format.

How are you currently handling API errors in your projects?

articles.title: I built a free, offline photo resizer for Pakistani government forms (FPSC, PPSC, NADRA) — here's what the forms actually require
articles.description: Every government form in Pakistan has a different photo rule, and none of them explain it well: FPSC...
articles.body_html:
Every government form in Pakistan has a different photo rule, and none of them explain it well: FPSC wants a JPG under 30 KB, PPSC under 25 KB, Pak Navy under 20 KB, the passport portal 350x467 pixels. A phone photo is 3 MB. Thousands of applications fail at the upload step every week.

So I built FormKB (https://formkb.com), a set of browser-only tools: the photo never leaves the device (Canvas API, no upload), and each form has a preset read from the organisation's own guidelines PDF, quoted on the page.

A few things I learned building it:

  1. The limits on blogs are often wrong. I read the official documents and found PPSC's "140x177" and NTS's "50 KB" repeated everywhere without a source. Every preset on the site links the PDF it came from: https://formkb.com/photo-size-requirements

  2. "KB" is not a pixel size. People search "20 KB photo size in pixels" constantly, so I wrote the conversion down with a table instead of a formula that doesn't exist: https://formkb.com/guides/kb-to-pixels

  3. Binary search on JPEG quality beats guessing. The resizer picks the largest pixel size and quality that still fits under the limit, in the browser, usually in under a second.

  4. The same engine works for other countries' forms once you have the official spec: UK passport (600x750 px, 50 KB–10 MB), Bangladesh Teletalk (300x300 under 100 KB), India's JEE Main (10–200 KB): https://formkb.com/jee-main-photo-signature-size

Stack: Next.js static export on Cloudflare, no backend, no analytics. Tests run the real tools in headless Chrome against the stated limits (252 checks).

If you've fought a government upload form, I'd like to hear which one; the next presets come from those stories.

articles.title: Building an Image Compressor That Hits an Exact File Size
articles.description: Every upload form has the same annoying quirk: it rejects on file size, but every compressor gives...
articles.body_html:
Every upload form has the same annoying quirk: it rejects on file size, but every compressor gives you a quality slider instead of a size input.

So you end up in a loop. Compress, check size, compress again. Adjust quality from 80 to 70. Check again. 65. Again.

I wanted to invert that: give the tool the number, let it figure out the quality.

The problem with quality-first

JPEG file size doesn't vary linearly with the quality parameter. Going from q=0.9 to q=0.8 might drop the file by 40%, or by 8%, depending on the image content. That's why the manual loop feels so random.

But the relationship is monotonic — lower quality always means smaller file. That's enough for a binary search.

Binary search over quality

For a fixed image size, find the highest quality whose encoded blob is still under the target:

async function encodeUnderTarget(canvas, mime, targetBytes) {
  // Check the ceiling first: if even q=0.95 fits, done.
  const top = await toBlob(canvas, mime, 0.95);
  if (top.size <= targetBytes) return { blob: top, quality: 0.95 };

  let lo = 0.15, hi = 0.95, best = null;

  // 6 iterations narrows the range to ~1% — plenty for file size.
  for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    const blob = await toBlob(canvas, mime, mid);
    if (blob.size <= targetBytes) {
      best = { blob, quality: mid };
      lo = mid;          // this works, try higher quality
    } else {
      hi = mid;          // too big, try lower
    }
  }
  return best;           // null means even q=0.15 is too big
}

function toBlob(canvas, mime, quality) {
  return new Promise((resolve) =>
    canvas.toBlob((blob) => resolve(blob), mime, quality)
  );
}

Six encodes lands within a few percent below the target, instead of the 20-40% below you get from guessing a quality value.

When quality isn't enough

Some images can't hit the target at any quality — high-ISO photos, heavy noise, complex texture. So there's a second loop: if even q=0.15 overshoots, scale down and retry.

let scale = 1;
for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 6; attempt++) {
  const canvas = drawScaled(img, srcW * scale, srcH * scale);
  const result = await encodeUnderTarget(canvas, mime, targetBytes);
  if (result) return { ...result, scale };

  scale *= 0.7;   // 30% smaller each round
  if (Math.max(srcW, srcH) * scale < 48) break;
}

The 0.7 factor matters. At 0.9 you need many more rounds, and each round costs 6 encodes.

Three things that bit me

1. Transparent PNGs turn black in JPEG

canvas.toBlob(..., 'image/jpeg') composites onto black by default. You have to paint white first:

ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
ctx.fillRect(0, 0, w, h);
ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0, w, h);

2. Huge images make the search unusable

Each toBlob() on a 24MP canvas takes 300-500ms. Six encodes × six scale rounds = 30+ seconds. So downscale anything above ~12MP before searching:

const MAX_PIXELS = 12e6;
if (srcW * srcH > MAX_PIXELS) {
  scale = Math.sqrt(MAX_PIXELS / (srcW * srcH));
}

3. Files already under target shouldn't be re-encoded

If your 20KB file is already under 50KB, re-encoding it loses quality for zero benefit. Pass it through untouched:

if (file.size <= targetBytes) {
  return { blob: file, scale: 1, passthrough: true };
}

Results

Input Target Output Time
1600×1200 photo, 148 KB 50 KB 49 KB ~1.4s
3000×2000 photo, 2.7 MB 50 KB 50 KB ~7s
1200×900 photo, 88 KB 20 KB 20 KB ~0.7s
240×180, 14 KB 50 KB unchanged ~0.1s

What I'd like to know

  • Is binary search the right approach? libjpeg does something similar internally but I wanted pure JS with no wasm payload. Is there a smarter rate-control strategy?
  • WebP vs JPEG: WebP wins 25-35% at equal quality, and it's my default. But Safari's WebP encode path was historically slow — anyone have current numbers?
  • The 12MP cutoff: arbitrary. Below it, search feels instant; above it, it drags. Is there a better heuristic?

The tool is at imgpress-c90.pages.dev — no upload endpoint exists, you can go offline after the page loads and it still works. Source is plain JS, no build step.

articles.title: Why One Emoji Breaks Your Coding Agent's TUI Borders: wcwidth vs Grapheme Clusters
articles.description: A 2025 emoji shifted Claude Code's TUI one cell until a width-table update. How wcwidth, VS16, ZWJ and mode 2027 decide where your agent's borders land.
articles.body_html:
• Book: AI That Acts
  • The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Paste 🫪 into Claude Code 2.1.207 and the text after it slides one cell to the right. That is the report in anthropics/claude-code#80475, opened July 23, 2026: stray characters bleeding into neighbouring rows, inverse-video blocks between words, and a mess that stays until Ctrl-L or a window resize forces a full repaint.

The emoji is U+1FAEA, DISTORTED FACE, which arrived with Unicode 17.0 in 2025. The terminal drew it two cells wide. Claude Code's width table was older than the emoji and counted fewer. In the maintainer's closing comment, the fix "came from updating the Unicode width tables in the runtime Claude Code ships with," and from 2.1.221 on, both 🫪 and 🫩 (U+1FAE9, FACE WITH BAGS UNDER EYES, reported later in the same thread) measure as two cells.

Claude Code and the terminal disagreed on how many columns U+1FAEA takes, and every cell after it inherited the gap.

Two programs, one grid

A terminal is a grid of cells. A TUI like Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI never sees that grid. It writes bytes, and to draw a box it has to predict where the cursor will be after each string. The right border of a box sits at "left edge plus the width I computed." The terminal then advances the cursor by the width it computed.

When those two numbers agree, borders line up. When they differ by one, everything the program draws after that character lands one column off, and every partial redraw targets the wrong cells. That is why these bugs show up as smearing and duplicated lines across the whole screen.

kitty's text sizing protocol docs put it bluntly: if the client program and the terminal disagree on cell counts, "the entire user interface can be broken".


The program and the terminal each measure the same character. One cell of disagreement moves every border after it.

Three counts, none of them is width

Start with what JavaScript can count. Save this as count.mjs and run it with node count.mjs:

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter("en", {
  granularity: "grapheme",
});

const samples = {
  ascii: "A",
  cjk: "中",
  heart: "\u{2764}",
  heartVS16: "\u{2764}\u{FE0F}",
  thumbTone: "\u{1F44D}\u{1F3FD}",
  family: "\u{1F468}\u{200D}\u{1F469}\u{200D}\u{1F467}",
  distorted: "\u{1FAEA}",
};

console.log("ICU Unicode:", process.versions.unicode);
for (const [name, s] of Object.entries(samples)) {
  const units = s.length;
  const points = [...s].length;
  const clusters = [...seg.segment(s)].length;
  console.log(name.padEnd(10), s, units, points, clusters);
}

.length counts UTF-16 code units. Spreading the string counts code points. Intl.Segmenter counts grapheme clusters, which UAX #29 defines as user-perceived characters. Its rule GB11 says: "Do not break within emoji modifier sequences or emoji zwj sequences."

The family is three emoji glued together by two ZERO WIDTH JOINERs (U+200D), so it is five code points and eight UTF-16 units but one grapheme, while the skin-tone thumbs-up and the heart followed by U+FE0F are two code points and one grapheme each.

A Chinese character is one code point and one grapheme, and it still takes two cells.

The first line prints the Unicode version your Node's ICU knows. The Node docs example shows unicode: '17.0'. Unicode 18.0 is dated September 16, 2026. Every program that measures width carries a snapshot of some version, and they are rarely the same snapshot.

Now draw a box the naive way, one cell per code point:

const rows = [
  "plain text",
  "中文",
  "\u{2764}\u{FE0F} ok",
  "\u{1F468}\u{200D}\u{1F469}\u{200D}\u{1F467} team",
];
const width = (s) => [...s].length;
const inner = 16;
const edge = "+" + "-".repeat(inner) + "+";

console.log(edge);
for (const r of rows) {
  console.log("|" + r + " ".repeat(inner - width(r)) + "|");
}
console.log(edge);

The plain-text row lines up. The 中文 row overshoots by two cells in every terminal, because each character is one code point and two cells. The heart and family rows are where terminals disagree: run the script in two emulators and compare where those right borders land.

Where width actually comes from

The width a terminal assigns usually starts from the East_Asian_Width property in UAX #11. Its values are A (ambiguous), F (fullwidth), H (halfwidth), N (neutral), Na (narrow) and W (wide). W and F take two cells, and W also covers "characters that have the UTS51 property Emoji_Presentation." For ambiguous characters the annex says: "If the context cannot be established reliably, they should be treated as narrow characters by default."

That covers single code points. Emoji sequences are where the tables run out. UTS #51 defines U+FE0F, VARIATION SELECTOR-16, as the character "used to request an emoji presentation." The plain heart U+2764 has no Emoji_Presentation, so on its own it is a text-style, one-cell character. Add VS16 and you ask for the two-cell emoji. A per-code-point width function sees one narrow character plus a variation selector that takes no cells of its own, and so the total depends on whether the function knows the sequence.

The Python wcwidth library documents exactly this split. wcwidth('\U00002640'), the plain ♀ (U+2640), is 1. wcswidth('\U00002640\U0000FE0F'), the same sign with VS16, is 2. Ask for VTE's behaviour with wcstwidth(..., term_program='vte') on that same VS16 string and the docs show 1. Its four-person family example measures 2 by default and 8 with term_program='alacritty', a correction the docs put down to Alacritty not supporting emoji ZWJ.

Here is the Python side of the same experiment:

# pip install --upgrade wcwidth
import unicodedata
from wcwidth import wcwidth, wcswidth

print("UCD", unicodedata.unidata_version)
for ch in ["A", "中", "\U00002764", "\U0001FAEA"]:
    eaw = unicodedata.east_asian_width(ch)
    print(f"U+{ord(ch):04X}", eaw, wcwidth(ch))

print(wcswidth("\U00002640\U0000FE0F"))  # wcwidth docs: 2

unicodedata follows the Python release, not the wcwidth package. The Python 3.15 docs say its data comes from UCD 17.0.0. An older interpreter or an older wcwidth will give a different answer for U+1FAEA, which is the same kind of mismatch as the Claude Code bug.

It goes the other way too. In gemini-cli#25369, Ink, the React renderer Gemini CLI draws with, used Intl.Segmenter to merge a Thai consonant and SARA AM (U+0E33) into one cluster of width 1, while tmux and xterm.js drew it across two columns. The symptom was one streamed line repeated 8 to 10 times and an input line that kept jumping down. It was closed as completed on October 23, 2026, via PR #29883. This time the program was the one counting by clusters, and the terminal in front of it counted differently.


A ZWJ sequence is several code points and one grapheme. Whether it takes two cells or eight depends on who is counting.

Mode 2027: asking the terminal to count graphemes

Some terminals now let a program opt into one shared rule. Contour's terminal-unicode-core spec defines DEC private mode 2027. CSI ? 2027 h turns it on, CSI ? 2027 l turns it off, and CSI ? 2027 $ p asks whether the terminal supports it. With the mode on, a grapheme cluster lives in one place on the grid, and a VS16 in the cluster promotes it to emoji presentation, which makes it two cells wide.

You can probe your terminal from Node:

process.stdin.setRawMode(true);
const timer = setTimeout(() => done("no reply"), 500);

function done(msg) {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  process.stdin.setRawMode(false);
  console.log(msg);
  process.exit(0);
}

process.stdin.once("data", (b) => done(JSON.stringify(String(b))));
process.stdout.write("\x1b[?2027$p");

The answer is a DECRPM report shaped like CSI ? 2027 ; Ps $ y. Ps 0 means the terminal doesn't recognise the mode, 1 means it is set, 2 means reset, 3 and 4 mean permanently set or reset. The timeout matters: a terminal that ignores the query sends nothing at all.

Support is uneven. In the ucs-detect results, which measure terminals by printing test strings and asking for the cursor position afterwards, Ghostty, WezTerm, foot and Windows Terminal report mode 2027. kitty, iTerm2, Alacritty and xterm.js do not. The page gives no test date and says results are provided as-is, so check the version next to each row.

Ghostty exposes the trade-off as a setting. grapheme-width-method defaults to unicode, which the docs call correct but able to desync the cursor with programs that measure the legacy wcswidth way. legacy matches those programs and can get skin-tone emoji wrong. A program that turns on mode 2027 forces unicode regardless. kitty went a different direction with OSC 66, where the program states the width with w= and the terminal stops guessing.

The two-pane test

Put two agent TUIs side by side and the disagreement becomes something you can locate. I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs every agent's own interface in a real terminal and lets you split panes right or down, so Claude Code and Codex can sit next to each other on the same screen.


Hermes IDE 2.3.4: Codex on orders-types and Claude Code on orders-api, side by side, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with the sessions sidebar showing status, context use, cost and branch.

Paste the same string with an emoji into both. Both panes live in the same app, so the terminal side of the comparison stays fixed. If one pane's border breaks and the other's holds, the difference is in the agents. Codex's TUI is built on Ratatui and pulls in the unicode-width and unicode-segmentation crates (its Cargo.toml), and Claude Code ships its own width tables in its runtime, so the two can carry different Unicode snapshots.

Then flip it. Run the same agent in a second terminal emulator. If the border is fine there, the agent agrees with that emulator and the first one is the odd one out. The rest is cheap:

  1. Update the agent first. claude update is the whole fix for #80475.
  2. Repaint with Ctrl-L or a resize to clear a smeared screen.
  3. Keep fresh emoji out of the strings an agent draws in its chrome: session names, branch names, status lines.
  4. If you write a TUI, measure grapheme clusters, query mode 2027 and turn it on when the reply shows the mode is recognised (Ps 1 or 2). Where it isn't, test against the terminals your users actually run.

Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It isn't affiliated with Nous Research, Anthropic, OpenAI or Google. Download it and the source is on GitHub.

Finding the character

Next time an agent's box comes out with a jagged right edge, skip the font settings and find the character just before the break. Compare the width your agent gives it with the width your terminal draws, then check which Unicode version each was built with. If the versions match, compare how each one segments that cluster; the Gemini CLI Thai bug was that kind.

If this was useful

If you're building your own agent in TypeScript, the terminal is only the surface. AI That Acts covers the part underneath it: tool calling, functions, and getting a first working agent to do real work in Node, so the thing drawing those borders has something worth showing.

It is book 3 of AI in TypeScript, a five-book series that runs from your first LLM call to agents in production.

articles.title: Why Object.keys(user) Returns string[], Not (keyof User)[]: TypeScript Means It
articles.description: The (keyof T)[] cast on Object.keys type-checks and indexes a key that isn't there. Why TypeScript refuses to change it, and four patterns that stay honest.
articles.body_html:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Object.keys(user) as (keyof User)[] sits in a lot of TypeScript codebases, usually in a utils file next to a comment that blames the compiler.

The TypeScript team has heard that complaint for about a decade. In May 2020, Ryan Cavanaugh of the TypeScript team wrote in a related issue that they "basically get a bug report or PR to change Object.keys to keyof T at least once a week" (microsoft/TypeScript#38520). The answer keeps being no, and it has been no since Anders Hejlsberg's objection on a 2016 pull request that tried to make the change (#12253).

The no is deliberate. Once you see the reason, the cast is where the bug lives.

The cast that type-checks and then throws

The declaration in TypeScript's own lib file is one line: keys(o: object): string[]; (lib.es5.d.ts). Here is the program everyone writes to get around it:

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

const labels: Record<keyof User, string> = {
  id: "ID",
  name: "Full name",
};

const row = { id: 1, name: "Ada", isAdmin: true };
const user: User = row; // compiles: row is not a fresh literal

const keys = Object.keys(user) as (keyof User)[];
for (const k of keys) {
  console.log(labels[k].toUpperCase());
}

This compiles under strict. Every line is legal. row has the type { id: number; name: string; isAdmin: boolean }, which is assignable to User because it has everything User asks for. The cast tells the compiler that keys holds only "id" and "name", so labels[k] is typed string and .toUpperCase() is allowed.

At runtime, user and row are the same object. Object.keys returns the object's own enumerable string-keyed property names, all of them, so it returns ["id", "name", "isAdmin"]. The loop prints two labels, then reaches isAdmin, reads labels["isAdmin"], gets undefined, and calls .toUpperCase() on it. That is a TypeError, in code the compiler signed off on because the as told it to.


A type lists what a value must have. The value can carry more.

Structural typing: User is a floor, not a ceiling

TypeScript checks shapes. A value is a User if it has an id: number and a name: string. Nothing in that rule says it can't have more. That is what makes structural typing pleasant day to day: you can pass a database row, a class instance or an API payload anywhere a narrower interface is expected, as long as the required fields are there.

The same rule turns (keyof User)[] into a false promise. Hejlsberg put it this way on the 2016 pull request: "an object can (and often does) have more properties at run-time than are statically known at compile time" (#12253). His example in the same thread was a Base type: calling Object.keys on a Base and getting (keyof Base)[] back "is almost certainly wrong because an actual instance would be a derived object with more keys".

You don't need inheritance to hit it. All of these hand a wider object to code that sees User:

  • a function render(u: User) called with a row variable that also carries role
  • JSON.parse(body) as User on a response that grew a field last sprint
  • an ORM row with createdAt and updatedAt that you typed as User
  • const withSession = { ...user, sessionId }, later passed to a User parameter

In every case keyof User is a lower bound on the runtime keys. Object.keys is the runtime telling you the truth, and string[] is the type that matches it.

What keyof actually computes

keyof is a type-level operator with its own rules, and several of them diverge from what Object.keys can return:

type K1 = keyof User;                     // "id" | "name"
type K2 = keyof { [k: string]: boolean }; // string | number
type K3 = keyof { [n: number]: unknown }; // number
type K4 = keyof { 0: string };            // 0
type K5 = keyof {};                       // never

K2 surprises people. The TypeScript handbook explains that with a string index signature, keyof gives string | number "because JavaScript object keys are always coerced to a string, so obj[0] is always the same as obj["0"]".

K4 goes the other way. Since TypeScript 2.9, keyof T is a subtype of string | number | symbol, and a number-like property name stays a number literal. Object.keys({ 0: "a" }) returns ["0"], a string. So even on an object with no extra properties, (keyof T)[] would put the number 0 in the type where the runtime gives you the string "0". Symbol keys show up in keyof and never in Object.keys, which returns only string-keyed properties (MDN).

K5 is the case Hejlsberg called degenerate: {} accepts almost any value, yet keyof {} is never, so a keyof-typed Object.keys would claim every such object has no keys at all (#12253).

Excess property checks only guard fresh literals

"But TypeScript does reject extra properties," you might say. It does, in one place. The handbook says "object literals get special treatment and undergo excess property checking when assigning them to other variables, or passing them as arguments" (Object Types). The same page shows the escape hatch: assign the object to another variable first, and the check no longer runs.

// Error: 'isAdmin' does not exist in type 'User'
const a: User = { id: 1, name: "Ada", isAdmin: true };

// Fine: same value, routed through a variable
const row = { id: 1, name: "Ada", isAdmin: true };
const b: User = row;

The check is a lint for typos at the moment you write a literal, and it can't follow a value across a function boundary. A real guarantee would need exact object types, which have been an open proposal since December 15, 2016 (#12936), still labelled "Awaiting More Feedback".

Until something like that ships, the language has no way to say "this User has exactly these keys", so Object.keys can't say it either.


Typed keys are safe when you control what goes into the container.

Four patterns that stay honest

The common thread: the key type comes from something you built.

1. Own the key list. Write the keys once as a tuple and iterate that, never the object.

const USER_FIELDS = ["id", "name"] as const satisfies
  readonly (keyof User)[];
type UserField = (typeof USER_FIELDS)[number];

function describe(u: User): string[] {
  return USER_FIELDS.map((k) => `${k}=${u[k]}`);
}

Extra properties on u are ignored because you never looked for them. The satisfies clause catches a typo in the list. It does not prove you listed every key; pattern 2 shows how to get that guarantee.

2. satisfies on a literal you wrote. The satisfies operator from TypeScript 4.9 validates "that the type of an expression matches some type, without changing the resulting type of that expression". On an object literal it runs the excess property check, and Record<keyof User, string> makes a missing key an error too.

const userLabels = {
  id: "ID",
  name: "Full name",
} satisfies Record<keyof User, string>;

// Only for objects you created as literals.
const literalKeys = <T extends object>(o: T) =>
  Object.keys(o) as (keyof T & string)[];

for (const k of literalKeys(userLabels)) {
  console.log(k, userLabels[k].toUpperCase());
}

This is still a cast. It is safe here only because the object is the literal you wrote three lines up and nothing adds keys to it. The & string drops the number and symbol members keyof can include. Pass a value typed User into literalKeys and you are back to the opening bug, which is why the helper's name says what it is for.

3. Use a Map and let it enforce the key type. MDN puts the difference plainly: "A Map does not contain any keys by default. It only contains what is explicitly put into it."

const labelMap = new Map<keyof User, string>([
  ["id", "ID"],
  ["name", "Full name"],
]);

for (const [k, label] of labelMap) {
  console.log(k, label.toUpperCase());
}

The constructor and set only accept keyof User keys, so the key type holds without a cast. labelMap.get(k) returns string | undefined, which is the correct type for a lookup.

4. Narrow strings from outside. For a parsed body or a query string, keep Object.keys as string[] and check each key against the list you own:

function isUserField(k: string): k is UserField {
  return (USER_FIELDS as readonly string[]).includes(k);
}

function logUserFields(input: Record<string, unknown>) {
  for (const k of Object.keys(input)) {
    if (isUserField(k)) console.log(k, input[k]);
  }
}

Unknown keys fall through instead of getting a type they never had.

Where to look first

Object.keys answers "what keys does this value have right now", and no static type can answer that for a structurally typed value. Grep your codebase for as (keyof and check where each value came from. If your code wrote it as a literal and nothing widened it since, the cast is fine. If it arrived through a parameter or a parsed body, it is the opening bug waiting for a wider object. The next time someone files the weekly Object.keys issue, the answer is already in #12253.

If this was useful

The trick in this post, telling the compiler's key type apart from the runtime's keys, sits at the heart of The TypeScript Type System. It goes deep on generics, mapped and conditional types and branded types, so you can write helpers like literalKeys and know exactly where they stop being true.

It is one of five books in The TypeScript Library. Books 1 and 2 are the core path; if you are coming from the JVM or PHP, book 3 or 4 covers that same ground from where you stand; book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Why We Ditched a 30MB AI Model and Built a <2.5ms Canvas Snapper in TypeScript
articles.description: How we replaced a 30MB Segment-Anything model with 200 lines of classical TypeScript, achieving <2.5ms canvas element-snapping with zero dependencies.
articles.body_html:
When building FocusFlow — a spatial storytelling canvas that turns architecture diagrams into 60fps cinematic presentations — we faced an intriguing computer vision problem: Click-to-Snap.

When a user imports a rasterized architecture diagram (PNG/JPEG/SVG) and clicks anywhere inside an element (like an ECS task card, a VPC boundary, or a database cylinder), the engine needs to extract its precise bounding box in < 5ms to smoothly anchor camera viewport frustums.

1. The Initial Mirage: WebGPU + MobileSAM

In 2026, the knee-jerk reaction for image segmentation in the browser is to reach for a machine learning model:

  • Run a quantized Segment Anything (MobileSAM) model via ONNX Runtime Web.
  • Offload inference to WebGPU.

The Real-World Costs:

  • Payload Penalty: An initial ~30MB model download.
  • VRAM Overhead: 250MB–350MB GPU buffer allocation.
  • Latency Friction: 120ms–180ms inference per click.
  • Failure Modes: Over-segmenting internal text lines or bleeding into complex canvas backgrounds.

For a lightweight web application that users open in their desktop browser, forcing a 30MB weight download just to detect rectangles felt like engineering malpractice.

We asked ourselves: Can classical computer vision, implemented in pure TypeScript and tuned for CSS geometry, beat neural nets in speed, accuracy, and footprint?

2. Five Real-World CSS Edge Cases That Break Naive Sobel

Traditional Sobel gradient filters assume simple solid shapes on clean contrast. But modern UI diagrams look nothing like that:

  1. Text Hole Perforation: Cards are packed with bold headers, monospace code snippets, and badge pills. High-frequency font glyph edges easily trick naive ray-casters into snapping to inner text.
  2. CSS Linear Gradients: Backgrounds subtly drift across 400px. Standard global thresholding either cuts off mid-card or bleeds across boundaries.
  3. Emoji & Colorful Badges: Clicking directly on an inline icon (e.g. 🛡️ or 🐘) corrupts single-point background color sampling.
  4. Long Title Blockades: A 24-character monospace title forms a contiguous horizontal boundary that cuts the card's flood-fill front in half.
  5. Dark-on-Dark Contrast: Dark-mode cards (#0f172a) against canvas backgrounds (#0c1220) yield miniscule perceptual color differences ($\Delta E < 25$) surrounded by diffuse drop shadows.

3. The Pure Math Architecture: A 3-Tier Pipeline

To solve this without machine learning, we built a 3-tier deterministic pipeline:

3.1 Compact 3-Ring Profiler (Phase 1.6)

Instead of single-point sampling, we sample 33 concentric points across 4 rings ($r \in [1, 8, 16, 24]\text{px}$). Each sample is weighted inversely by its local Sobel gradient flatness:
$$W_i = \max(1, 35 - G_i)$$
High-gradient text pixels are suppressed, while flat card pixels dominate. If a cluster fails validation, a Top-3 candidate fallback loop recovers the true background.

3.2 Floating Gradient BFS

Rather than comparing against an absolute seed color, our BFS tracks local step-to-step color deviation ($\Delta E_{\text{step}} \le 8$).

  • On flat background pixels, expensive $3 \times 3$ Sobel convolution is bypassed entirely.
  • This optimization dropped BFS runtime from 106ms down to 1.8ms (a 58x speedup).

3.3 Spatially Separable Anisotropic Morphological Closing

To seal text perforations without blurring vertical card edges, we employ an anisotropic separable kernel:

  • Horizontal kernel ($r_x = 6\text{px}$): Locks tight around card borders.
  • Vertical kernel ($r_y = 14\text{px}$): Bridges across multi-line text lines and headers. Because the 2D kernel is mathematically separable into 1D passes, algorithmic complexity drops from $O(K^2)$ to $O(2K)$, saving 90% of active pixel computations.

4. Memory & Zero-GC Guarantees

JavaScript garbage collection pauses are the enemy of smooth 60fps canvas interaction.

  • All intermediate masks and flood-fill queues utilize pre-allocated Uint8Array and Float32Array pools.
  • Total heap footprint is strictly capped under 450 KB.
  • Result: 0 GC collections during click-and-drag interactions.

5. Benchmarks & Industrial Validation

Across our 20-suite automated E2E test matrix (including nested cloud diagrams, dark-mode wireframes, and accent-bar cards):

  • End-to-End Latency: < 2.5ms
  • TypedArray Memory: < 450 KB
  • External Dependencies: 0 KB
  • Pass Rate: 20 / 20 PASS (100%)

Conclusion

Sometimes the most scalable engineering decision in 2026 is not to deploy a transformer model. For structured UI domains, classical computer vision combined with modern TypedArrays delivers 60x faster performance with zero bundle bloat.

Our full architecture and implementation details are open-sourced:

  • Repository: https://github.com/tumio-ltd/focusflow
  • Live Demo: https://focusflow.tumio.site

articles.title: Streaming Markdown in Vue: Rendering LLM Tokens Without Flicker
articles.description: Every AI chat UI hits the same wall. Tokens arrive over SSE, you do content += token, and a computed...
articles.body_html:
Every AI chat UI hits the same wall. Tokens arrive over SSE, you do content += token, and a computed property calls marked.parse(content) again. For a short answer it works. For a 3,000-token answer with a table, a fenced code block, and a Mermaid diagram, the message area re-renders dozens of times per second. The result is flicker, jumping scroll position, diagrams that vanish until the closing fence arrives, and a main thread that stays busy long after the stream ends.

I maintain markstream-vue, a streaming Markdown renderer built for exactly this case. This post walks through why the usual renderer pipeline struggles with token streams, and what a streaming-first renderer does differently.

The problem isn't Markdown. It's the timing.

marked, markdown-it, and react-markdown are excellent at rendering a finished document. Their contract is: give me valid Markdown, I give you HTML or a component tree.

An LLM stream violates that contract constantly. Mid-stream you have:

  • an unclosed **bold run,
  • a code fence with no closing backticks,
  • half a table,
  • $$ math with no closing delimiter,
  • a Mermaid block that only becomes parseable at the very end.

If you re-parse and re-render the full string on every token, you pay for the entire document each time. If you pass partial Markdown straight to a finished-document renderer, you get either broken output or a loading state that flashes on every chunk.

What streaming-first actually changes

Markstream keeps the incomplete state as a first-class idea instead of an error case.

1. Two render modes for two different UX goals

Mode Config Best for
Virtual window (default) max-live-nodes="220" Long answers, docs, chat history — steady scrolling and memory
Incremental batches max-live-nodes="0" The "typing" feel — new content flows in small slices

The virtual window keeps a sliding set of mounted nodes, so a 10,000-block document doesn't mean 10,000 live DOM nodes. Incremental mode disables virtualization and renders in small batches, which is usually what you want for a chat bubble that is actively growing.

2. Heavy blocks settle progressively

Mermaid and KaTeX are optional peers, not bundled dependencies. When they are installed, diagrams can render as soon as the syntax is complete, and update when later chunks change them — rather than blocking the whole message until the stream ends.

Code blocks are the other hot spot. In v2, the enhanced code surface comes from the optional stream-diffs peer; without it you get a plain <pre> fallback. That keeps the default install small and lets you opt into the heavier diff/highlighting surface only where you need it.

3. final is a real state, not a guess

Most flicker bugs come from not knowing whether the stream is done. Markstream takes a final prop. While it is false, the parser assumes unfinished constructs are still loading. When it flips to true, the renderer invalidates the streaming cache and reparses with final semantics, so a trailing $$ or an unclosed fence doesn't stay stuck in a loading state forever.

Quick start 

pnpm add markstream-vue

<script setup lang="ts">
import MarkdownRender from 'markstream-vue'
import 'markstream-vue/index.css'
</script>

<template>
  <MarkdownRender :content="markdown" />
</template>

That is the whole integration for a read-only surface. For an AI chat message, add the stream state:

<script setup lang="ts">
import { onBeforeUnmount, ref } from 'vue'
import MarkdownRender from 'markstream-vue'
import 'markstream-vue/index.css'

const content = ref('')
const final = ref(false)
let source: EventSource | undefined

function start(url: string) {
  source = new EventSource(url)
  source.onmessage = (event) => {
    content.value += event.data
  }
  source.addEventListener('done', () => {
    final.value = true
    source?.close()
  })
}

onBeforeUnmount(() => source?.close())
</script>

<template>
  <MarkdownRender
    :content="content"
    :final="final"
    :max-live-nodes="0"
    :render-batch-size="16"
    :render-batch-delay="8"
    :fade="false"
    :typewriter="true"
  />
</template>

:max-live-nodes="0" selects incremental mode. The batch props control how much work is allowed per frame, which is the difference between a smooth typewriter effect and one that jumps in 2 KB chunks.

If you already parse Markdown on the server or in a worker, you can skip client-side parsing entirely and pass typed nodes:

import { getMarkdown, parseMarkdownToStructure } from 'markstream-vue'

const md = getMarkdown()
const nodes = parseMarkdownToStructure(source, md, { final: true })

<MarkdownRender :nodes="nodes" />

That is also the escape hatch for SSR and hydration: parse once on the server, serialize the nodes, and keep streaming later chunks on the client.

Putting Vue components inside Markdown

This is the part that made the library worth building for me. A chat answer often needs a callout, a button, or a chart — something that isn't expressible in plain Markdown.

setCustomComponents maps a marker to a Vue component:

import { setCustomComponents } from 'markstream-vue'

setCustomComponents('chat', {
  CALLOUT: () => import('./Callout.vue'),
})

Then emit the marker in Markdown and scope the renderer:

[[CALLOUT:warning title="Heads up" body="This response was truncated."]]

<MarkdownRender :content="content" custom-id="chat" />

The same mechanism handles custom HTML tags such as thinking, with the original payload kept on the node.

When not to use it

I would rather you pick the right tool:

  • Static docs, blog posts, changelogs — marked or markdown-it is simpler and smaller. There is no stream to optimize.
  • You need every ecosystem plugin — the unified/remark ecosystem is hard to beat for finished documents.
  • You want zero optional peers — Markstream works, but Mermaid, KaTeX, and the enhanced code surface are opt-in for a reason.

The value shows up when Markdown is still changing while the user is reading it. That is a different rendering problem from "render this file".

Other frameworks

The same core is available outside Vue: markstream-react (React / Next.js), markstream-solid, markstream-svelte, markstream-angular, markstream-vue2, plus stream-markdown-parser for parsing without a UI layer.

Try it

  • Live Vue playground: https://markstream-vue.simonhe.me/
  • Shareable repro / test page: https://markstream-vue.simonhe.me/test
  • Docs: https://markstream.simonhe.me/frameworks/vue
  • GitHub: https://github.com/Simon-He95/markstream-vue
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/markstream-vue

If you have a streaming UI that flickers, the test page lets you paste a repro and share the URL — that is the fastest way to show me the bug.

Prefer the short version first? I wrote an earlier, shorter post on why streaming AI chat needs a renderer for incomplete Markdown: https://dev.to/simonhe95/why-streaming-ai-chat-needs-a-renderer-for-incomplete-markdown-4754

Disclosure: I am the maintainer of markstream-vue, so read the comparison with the usual grain of salt. The library is MIT-licensed, and the optional peers are the only paid-in-bundle-size trade-offs.

articles.body_html:
Mastering INP: How We Achieved Sub-10ms Input Latency Across 30 Reactive Web Tools

Have you ever typed into an input field on a modern web application, dragged a slider, or switched tabs, and felt a perceptible, jarring micro-stutter?

You hit a key, but the letter doesn't appear for 80 milliseconds. You drag a range slider, and the thumb jumps erratically across the track. You paste a paragraph of text, and the browser freezes entirely while the main thread turns completely red in Chrome DevTools.

In modern frontend development, we have normalized this input latency as the price of doing business with modern component frameworks.

Google made Interaction to Next Paint (INP) an official Core Web Vital, replacing First Input Delay (FID). While FID only measured the delay of the first interaction on a page, INP measures the latency of every single click, tap, and keypress throughout the entire user session. To pass Google's threshold, your 75th percentile of interactions must present a visual frame in under 200 milliseconds—with 50ms being the target for elite software.

When building Urban Mixo, a suite of 30 computational utilities and developer tools, our requirement was stricter:

Every calculation, keystroke, and slider adjustment must commit a visual frame within a 16.6ms budget (60 FPS)—running entirely on the user's device.

Here is an architectural deep dive into how we eliminated layout thrashing, virtual DOM diffing penalties, and JavaScript execution bottlenecks to achieve a consistent sub-10ms INP across 30 interactive mathematical engines.

1. The Virtual DOM Reconciliation Tax on High-Frequency Input

To understand why so many modern web utilities feel sluggish, examine how conventional component libraries (React, Vue) process high-frequency user interactions:

User Keystroke -> Event Listener -> State Dispatch -> Hook Trigger -> 
Virtual DOM Tree Re-creation -> Diffing Algorithm -> Batch DOM Commit -> Paint

When building an application like our 1-Minute Typing Speed Test—where competitive typists exceed 120 words per minute (over 10 distinct keystrokes per second)—this abstraction pipeline completely breaks down.

If each keystroke triggers a component re-render, virtual DOM comparison, and reconciliation pass across 500 individual character nodes, the scripting execution time regularly consumes 30ms to 60ms of CPU time per character. The browser misses multiple 16.6ms VSync refresh windows, queuing up pending keystrokes in the Task Queue and resulting in noticeable typing lag.

The Solution: Direct Node Caching & Targeted Mutation

Instead of maintaining a virtual representation of the DOM tree, we query and cache direct hardware references to exact visual nodes upon initialization. When an input event fires, we bypass tree diffing entirely and mutate the target style property or text node directly:

/**
 * Direct DOM Pointer Cache
 * Eliminates querySelector overhead and virtual tree diffing passes
 */
const DOM = {
  input: document.getElementById('typing-input'),
  displayWpm: document.getElementById('live-wpm-display'),
  displayAcc: document.getElementById('live-acc-display'),
  // Cache individual character span references in memory
  charSpans: []
};

// Initialize reference cache once during DOMContentLoaded
function initializeCharacterPointers(totalChars) {
  DOM.charSpans = new Array(totalChars);
  for (let i = 0; i < totalChars; i++) {
    DOM.charSpans[i] = document.getElementById(`ch-${i}`);
  }
}

// Sub-millisecond keystroke handler: 0.2ms execution budget
function handleKeystrokeDirect(currentIndex, isCorrect) {
  const targetNode = DOM.charSpans[currentIndex];
  if (!targetNode) return;

  // Direct class list mutation without tree traversal
  targetNode.className = isCorrect ? 'c-correct' : 'c-error';
}

By decoupling character validation from component tree re-renders, individual keystroke processing dropped from 35ms in our React prototype down to 0.4ms in vanilla JavaScript, entirely eliminating input lag during fast typing bursts.

2. Preventing Forced Synchronous Layouts (Layout Thrashing)

The second most common cause of high INP scores is layout thrashing. This occurs when JavaScript repeatedly interleaves DOM writes (changing styles, text, or classes) with DOM reads (requesting geometric metrics like offsetWidth, clientHeight, or getBoundingClientRect):

// DANGEROUS PATTERN: Causes multiple synchronous reflows
elements.forEach(el => {
  const width = el.offsetWidth; // READ (Forces browser to compute layout)
  el.style.width = (width + 10) + 'px'; // WRITE (Invalidates current layout)
});

When the browser encounters a layout read immediately following a write, it cannot wait for the next frame. It is forced to drop everything and execute a Forced Synchronous Layout on the main thread, freezing the user interface.

The Solution: Phased Read/Write Batching with requestAnimationFrame

In utilities with complex visual state—such as our Aspect Ratio & Dimension Resizer, which dynamically scales on-screen bounding boxes while recalculating Euclidean GCD ratios—we strictly batch geometric reads and writes:

let pendingAnimation = null;

function updateDimensionPreview(newWidth, newHeight, ratioX, ratioY) {
  // If an animation frame is already queued, cancel to prevent event flooding
  if (pendingAnimation) {
    cancelAnimationFrame(pendingAnimation);
  }

  // Schedule the DOM write for the exact start of the browser's next refresh cycle
  pendingAnimation = requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    // BATCH 1: Perform all computations in-memory
    const maxBoxW = 260;
    const maxBoxH = 170;
    let boxW = maxBoxW;
    let boxH = Math.round(boxW * (newHeight / newWidth));

    if (boxH > maxBoxH) {
      boxH = maxStageH;
      boxW = Math.round(boxH * (newWidth / newHeight));
    }

    // BATCH 2: Mutate DOM properties sequentially without reading back
    DOM.ratioBox.style.width = `${boxW}px`;
    DOM.ratioBox.style.height = `${boxH}px`;
    DOM.previewLabel.textContent = `${ratioX} : ${ratioY}`;

    pendingAnimation = null;
  });
}

By confining visual resizes to native requestAnimationFrame boundaries, the browser processes slider inputs asynchronously, guaranteeing that the Compositor thread never drops a frame.

3. Offloading Heavy Linguistic Math: The Real-Time Word Counter

Our Universal Word Counter & Text Analyzer does not simply count whitespace spaces. With every keystroke, it computes:

  1. Exact character, sentence, and paragraph arrays.
  2. Syllable counts per word to solve the algebraic Flesch Reading Ease formula: $$\text{Score} = 206.835 - 1.015 \left(\frac{\text{words}}{\text{sentences}}\right) - 84.6 \left(\frac{\text{syllables}}{\text{words}}\right)$$
  3. Stop-word filtering across a 150-word dictionary.
  4. Top-5 keyword density ratios sorted by frequency.

Running regex parsers and dynamic frequency sort trees across a 5,000-word essay on every single input event will inevitably block the main thread for 150ms+ if not engineered carefully.

The Solution: Event Loop Yielding via Cooperative Scheduling

Instead of letting heavy tokenization block the immediate rendering of the typed letter, we prioritize the immediate input paint and defer the complex linguistic analytics using an immediate microtask or scheduler.yield():

let analysisTimeout = null;

function handleTextInput(event) {
  // PHASE 1: Synchronous Critical Path (Target: < 2ms)
  // Update raw character count immediately so user feels instant feedback
  const rawText = DOM.textarea.value;
  DOM.charCountDisplay.textContent = rawText.length.toLocaleString();

  // PHASE 2: Cooperative Analytical Path
  // Clear any existing analytical run to debounce during fast typing
  if (analysisTimeout) {
    clearTimeout(analysisTimeout);
  }

  // Yield execution back to the browser's render pipeline
  analysisTimeout = setTimeout(() => {
    runFullLinguisticAnalysis(rawText);
  }, 35); // 35ms debounced window allows fast typing bursts without freezing
}

function runFullLinguisticAnalysis(text) {
  const words = text.trim() ? text.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean) : [];
  const sentences = text.trim() ? text.split(/[.!?]+(?:\s+|$)/).filter(Boolean) : [];

  // Execute Flesch Readability and Top-5 Density mapping...
  computeFleschIndex(words, sentences);
  computeKeywordDensity(words);
}

Because Phase 1 updates the immediate typing context in 0.3ms, the browser commits the frame instantly, registering an INP score of 4ms. The computationally heavier reading grade and density sorting finish milliseconds later without dropping a single visual frame.

4. Hardware-Accelerated Math: 60 FPS Canvas Plotting

In our Scientific Graphing Calculator, users plot continuous mathematical functions $f(x)$ (such as polynomials, trigonometrics, and parabolas) while zooming and panning across a Cartesian coordinate plane.

Building this with SVG DOM nodes (<path>, <circle>, <line>) creates extreme DOM overhead. A grid with 200 tick lines and a smooth 1,000-point curve represents over 1,200 unique SVG elements. Dragging or zooming requires the browser to recalculate styles and update layout geometry for all 1,200 nodes simultaneously.

The Solution: Immediate-Mode 2D Canvas Context

We replaced SVG DOM elements entirely with an immediate-mode HTML5 <canvas> rendering pipeline:

/**
 * 60 FPS Immediate-Mode Mathematical Function Plotter
 * Evaluates points in memory and pushes raw pixels directly to the GPU
 */
function renderGraphPlane(mathFunction, scale, originX, originY) {
  const width = canvas.width;
  const height = canvas.height;

  // Clear previous frame buffer
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height);

  // 1. Draw Cartesian Coordinate Grid
  drawGridLines(width, height, scale, originX, originY);

  // 2. Continuous Path Generation
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.lineWidth = 2.5;
  ctx.strokeStyle = '#4f46e5';

  let isFirstPoint = true;

  // Evaluate across pixel columns directly
  for (let px = 0; px < width; px += 2) {
    const mathX = (px - originX) / scale;
    const mathY = mathFunction(mathX);

    if (!isNaN(mathY) && isFinite(mathY)) {
      const py = originY - (mathY * scale);

      if (py >= -100 && py <= height + 100) {
        if (isFirstPoint) {
          ctx.moveTo(px, py);
          isFirstPoint = false;
        } else {
          ctx.lineTo(px, py);
        }
      } else {
        isFirstPoint = true;
      }
    } else {
      isFirstPoint = true;
    }
  }

  // Single GPU draw call for the entire curve
  ctx.stroke();
}

Because Canvas 2D is an immediate-mode rasterizer, there are zero DOM nodes in the tree. The browser evaluates the math function across 400 columns, executes a single ctx.stroke() draw call, and hands the frame directly to the GPU compositor in less than 2.8ms.

5. The Performance Benchmark Results

By systematically applying these principles across all 30 tools in our suite—from our Master Percentage Calculator Hub to our Work Hours & Timesheet Engine—our production Core Web Vitals telemetry demonstrates:

Google Chrome User Experience & DevTools Performance Audit:
------------------------------------------------------------
• Interaction to Next Paint (INP):    8 ms   (Target: < 200 ms)
• Total Blocking Time (TBT):           0 ms   (Target: < 200 ms)
• Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS):       0.000  (Target: < 0.10)
• First Contentful Paint (FCP):        0.8 s  (Target: < 1.8 s)
• JavaScript Execution Time:           < 4 ms per interaction
• Total Runtime Memory Footprint:      ~14 MB

6. Architectural Checklist for Sub-10ms Web Applications

If you are building data-heavy or interactive web tools, consider this architectural checklist:

  1. Avoid Virtual DOM on high-frequency input streams: For typing tests, real-time sliders, and drawing canvases, target the specific DOM node directly or use immediate-mode Canvas 2D.
  2. Never read layout metrics immediately after a write: Separate your calculations, batch your DOM updates, and use requestAnimationFrame for visual animations.
  3. Split critical paths from analytical paths: Update the user's immediate input synchronously in $< 2\text{ms}$, and defer complex algorithmic evaluations (readability scores, density sorting, stats) behind cooperative scheduling.
  4. Cache node references: Avoid querying the DOM tree repeatedly inside event listeners. Query once during initialization and preserve direct pointer references.
